Griffith]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kizirian |first=Shari |date=2020-01-20 |title=1917: The Year That Changed the Movies |url=https://silentfilm.org/1917-the-year-that-changed-the-movies/ |access-date=2026-07-01 |website=San Francisco Silent Film Festival |language=en-US}}</ref> in ''[[The Birth of a Nation]]'' (1915) and [[Intolerance (film)|''Intolerance'']] (1916).<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2019-05-30 |title=The 47th Best Director of All-Time: D.W. Griffith |url=https://thecinemaarchives.com/2019/05/30/the-47th-best-director-of-all-time-d-w-griffith/ |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=The Cinema Archives |language=en-US}}</ref> However, in the 1920s, European filmmakers such as [[Sergei Eisenstein]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-11-27 |title=Sergei Eisenstein: Films That Shook the World |url=https://bampfa.org/program/sergei-eisenstein-films-shook-world |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=BAMPFA |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ashley |date=2024-12-13 |title=The Lost Films of Sergei Eisenstein: A Window into Cinema's Alternative History |url=https://cornellpress.cornell.edu/lost-films-of-eisensteinan-imaginary-cinema-dustin-condren-12-13-2024/ |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=Cornell University Press |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau|F. W. Murnau]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-12 |title=F. W. Murnau: Voyages into the Imaginary |url=https://bampfa.org/program/f-w-murnau-voyages-imaginary |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=BAMPFA |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau 1888-1931 |url=https://www.dhm.de/lemo/biografie/wilhelm-friedrich-murnau |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=www.dhm.de |language=de}}</ref> and [[Fritz Lang]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-10-25 |title=Fritz Lang & German Expressionism |url=https://bampfa.org/program/fritz-lang-german-expressionism |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=BAMPFA |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-12-04 |title=Fritz Lang: 10 essential films |url=https://www.bfi.org.uk/lists/fritz-lang-10-essential-films |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=BFI |language=en}}</ref> in many ways inspired by the meteoric wartime progress of film through Griffith,{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} along with the contributions of actors like [[Charles Chaplin|Charles "Charlie" Chaplin]], [[Buster Keaton]], and others, quickly caught up with American film-making and continued to further advance the medium.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2009-11-13 |title=United Artists created |url=https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-5/united-artists-created |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=HISTORY |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Ferrier |first=Aimee |date=2023-02-27 |title=Was 1927 the most revolutionary year for cinema? |url=https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/1927-revolutionary-year-for-cinema/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=faroutmagazine.co.uk |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== 1920s–1960s: Evolution in sound ===
In the late 1920s,<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |title=Edison Shows the First Talking Pictures {{!}} Film {{!}} Research Starters {{!}} EBSCO Research |url=https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/film/edison-shows-first-talking-pictures |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=EBSCO |language=en}}</ref> the development of electronic [[sound recording and reproduction|sound recording]] technologies made it practical to incorporate a [[soundtrack]] of speech, music, and [[sound effects]] synchronized with the action on the screen.<ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=admin |date=2021-11-08 |title=What Was The First Film With Sound? |url=https://macksennettstudios.net/what-was-the-first-film-with-sound/ |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=Mack Sennett Studios |language=en-US}}</ref> The resulting [[sound film]]s were initially distinguished from the usual silent "moving pictures" or "movies" by calling them "talking pictures" or "talkies."<ref>{{Cite web |title=When did the Silent Film Era End? |url=https://kodakdigitizing.com/blogs/news/when-did-the-silent-film-era-end |access-date=2025-07-15 |website=Kodak Digitizing}}</ref><ref name=":8" /> The revolution they brought was swift. By 1931, silent film was practically extinct in the U.S.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=The Silent Film Era |url=https://movingimage.org/collection/the-silent-film-era/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=Museum of the Moving Image |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":9" /> and already being referred to as "the old medium."<ref name=":10" /> As of 2013, only 14% of America's silent feature films from 1912 to 1929 existed in their original format.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=Barnes |first=Mike |date=2013-12-04 |title='Alarming' Study Shows Just How Few Silent Films Have Survived |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/alarming-study-shows-just-how-661810/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Child |first=Ben |date=2013-12-04 |title=Vast majority of Hollywood silent films lost forever, study confirms |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2013/dec/04/american-silent-films-lost-forever |access-date=2026-07-06 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

[[File:The_Jazz_Singer_(1927).webm|thumbtime=16|thumb|Sound in cinema started gaining acceptance with movies like ''[[The Jazz Singer]]'' (1927)]]

The evolution of sound in cinema began with the idea of combining moving images with existing [[phonograph]] sound technology. Early sound-film systems, such as Thomas Edison's [[Kinetoscope]]<ref name=":11" /><ref name=":12" /> and the [[Vitaphone]] used by [[Warner Bros.|Warner Bros]].,<ref name=":8" /><ref name=":10" /> laid the groundwork for synchronized sound in film. The Vitaphone system, produced alongside [[Bell Telephone Company]] and [[Western Electric]], faced initial resistance due to expensive equipping costs, but sound in cinema gained acceptance with movies like [[Don Juan (1926 film)|''Don Juan'']] (1926) and ''[[The Jazz Singer]]'' (1927).<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |title=A brief history of sound in film |url=https://blog.scienceandmediamuseum.org.uk/brief-history-of-sound-in-film/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=National Science and Media Museum blog |date=13 September 2021 |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=Experimentation with Sound {{!}} MoMA |url=https://www.moma.org/collection/terms/film/experimentation-with-sound |access-date=2025-07-15 |website=The Museum of Modern Art |language=en}}</ref>

Meanwhile, Europe standardized on [[Tobis Film|Tobis-Klangfilm]] and [[Tri-Ergon]] systems.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Emergence of German Sound Film {{!}} filmportal.de |url=https://www.filmportal.de/en/topic/the-emergence-of-german-sound-film |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=www.filmportal.de}}</ref> This new technology allowed for greater fluidity in film, giving rise to more complex and epic movies like ''[[King Kong (1933 film)|King Kong]]'' (1933).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Sonnenschein |first=David |title=Sound Design: The Expressive Power of Music, Voice and Sound Effects in Cinema |year=2001}}</ref><ref name=":13" />

As the threat of [[television]] emerged in the 1940s and 1950s,<ref>{{Cite web |title=TV Milestones {{!}} American Experience |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/bigdream-tv-milestones/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=www.pbs.org |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":14">{{Cite web |last=Blakemore |first=Erin |date=2018-01-03 |title=How TV Killed Hollywood's Golden Age |url=https://www.history.com/articles/how-tv-killed-hollywoods-golden-age |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=HISTORY |language=en}}</ref> the film industry needed to innovate to attract audiences. In terms of sound technology, this meant the development of surround sound and more sophisticated audio systems,<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |last=Fore |first=Kait |date=2023-06-28 |title=Dolby Stereo and Surround Sound: The Evolution of Immersive Audio in the Film Industry |url=https://motionpicture.edu/socialcinema/2023/06/28/dolby-stereo-and-surround-sound-immersive-audio-in-film/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=Social Cinema |language=en-US}}</ref> such as [[Cinerama Releasing Corporation|Cinerama's]] seven-channel system.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-08-18 |title=Evolution of Surround Sound |url=https://www.studio11chicago.com/evolution-of-surround-sound/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=STUDIO 11 |language=en-US}}</ref> However, these advances required a large number of personnel to operate the equipment and maintain the sound experience in theaters.<ref name=":0" /> As an extra step, major film studios also started buying interests in TV stations, gaining a majority control of television studios by 1948.<ref name=":14" />

In 1966, [[Dolby Laboratories]] introduced the Dolby A noise reduction system, which became a standard in the recording industry and eliminated the hissing sound associated with earlier standardization efforts. [[Dolby Stereo]], a revolutionary surround sound system that was introduced audiences by 1977,<ref name=":15" /> followed and allowed cinema designers to take acoustics into consideration when designing theaters. This innovation enabled audiences in smaller venues to enjoy comparable audio experiences to those in larger city theaters.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The History and Science of Sound |url=https://tsdca.org/history/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=TSDCA |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== 1930s: Evolution in color ===
A significant technological advancement in film was the introduction of "natural [[color]]," where color was captured directly from nature through photography, as opposed to being manually added to black-and-white prints using techniques like hand-coloring or stencil-coloring.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Bordwell, David, Thompson, Smith |title=Film Art: An Introduction |publisher=New York: McGraw-Hill |year=2017 |edition=11th}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=davidbordwell.net : home |url=https://www.davidbordwell.net/ |access-date=2023-03-24 |website=www.davidbordwell.net}}</ref> Early color processes often produced colors that appeared far from "natural".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Usai, Paolo |title=Silent Cinema: An Introduction |publisher=London: BFI Publishing |year=2000 |edition=Rev.}}</ref> Unlike the rapid transition from silent films to sound films, color's replacement of black-and-white happened more gradually.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gunning |first=Tom |title=In Early Cinema: Space, Frame, Narrative, edited by Thomas Elsaesser |publisher=London: BFI Publishing |year=1994 |pages=239–247}}</ref>

A crucial innovation was the three-strip version of the Technicolor process, first used in animated cartoons in 1932.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Layton, Pierce |first=James, David |title=The Dawn of Technicolor 1915–1935 |publisher=NY: George Eastman Museum |year=1998 |pages=9–35}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Dawn of Technicolor, 1915–1935 |url=https://www.eastman.org/technicolor/book}}</ref> The process was later applied to live-action short films, specific sequences in feature films, and finally, for an entire feature film, ''[[Becky Sharp (film)|Becky Sharp]]'', in 1935.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Haines |first=Richard |title=Technicolor Movies: The History of Dye Transfer Printing |publisher=Jefferson, NC: McFarland & Company |year=1993}}</ref><ref name=":16">{{Cite web |date=2015-04-21 |title=A History of Colour: The Difficult Transition from Black and White Cinematography |url=https://the-artifice.com/history-of-colour-film/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=the-artifice.com |language=en}}</ref> Although the process was expensive, the positive public response, as evidenced by increased box office revenue, generally justified the additional cost.<ref name=":1" /> Consequently, the number of films made in color gradually increased year after year.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Higgins |first=Scott |title=Harnessing the Technicolor Rainbow: Color Design in the 1930s |publisher=Austin, TX: University of Texas Press |year=2007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Who We Are |url=https://www.technicolor.com/company/who-we-are |access-date=2023-03-24 |website=www.technicolor.com |language=en}}</ref> One of the first [[Blockbuster (entertainment)|mainstream films]] to use color was ''[[The Wizard of Oz]]'' (1939).<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Wizard of Oz triumphantly realized in Technicolor |url=https://www.technicolor.com/about/history/the-wizard-of-oz/ |access-date=2025-07-15 |website=Technicolor Group |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Martinez |first=Sandro |date=2025-02-24 |title=How The Wizard of Oz Revolutionized Color Film: Technicolor's Legacy Explained |url=https://pixflow.net/blog/how-the-wizard-of-oz-revolutionized-color-film-the-technicolor-legacy-explained/ |access-date=2025-07-15 |website=Pixflow Blog |language=en}}</ref>

=== 1950s: Growing influence of television ===
[[File:Night_of_the_Living_Dead_(1968).webm|thumb|left|''[[Night of the Living Dead]]'' (1968) has been listed as one of the most influential [[horror film]]s ever made.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-01-18 |title=Empire Features |url=http://www.empireonline.com/500/21.asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120118222018/http://www.empireonline.com/500/21.asp |archive-date=2012-01-18 |access-date=2022-06-24}}</ref>]]

In the early 1950s, [[black-and-white television]] started receiving criticism, with many believing that TV failed to reach the lofty intellectual and cultural expectations that accompanied its introduction.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Criticism of 1950s Television – 20th Century History Song Book |url=https://20thcenturyhistorysongbook.com/song-book/the-fifties/criticism-of-1950s-television/ |access-date=2025-07-15 |language=en-US}}</ref> In an attempt to lure audiences back to theaters, bigger screens,<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Big Idea-How to Marry a Millionaire |url=https://www.tcm.com/articles/961403/the-big-idea-how-to-marry-a-millionaire |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=Turner Classic Movies |language=en-us}}</ref> [[widescreen]] processes,<ref>{{Cite web |last=University |first=Columbia |title=Columbia Film Language Glossary: Cinerama |url=https://filmglossary.ccnmtl.columbia.edu/term/cinerama/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=filmglossary.ccnmtl.columbia.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Premiere of the First CinemaScope Film |url=https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/film/premiere-first-cinemascope-film |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=EBSCO |language=en}}</ref> [[polarized 3D system|polarized 3D projection]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Landler |first=Edward |date=2010-01-01 |title=It Came Right Out of the Movie Screen: A Look at 3-D Movies of the 50's - |url=https://cinemontage.org/came-right-movie-screen-look-3-d-movies-50s/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |language=en-US}}</ref> and [[stereophonic sound]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fratini |first=Dawn |date=2020-04-02 |title=Scale and Spectacle: AC In the 1950s |url=https://theasc.com/article/scale-and-spectacle/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=The American Society of Cinematographers |language=en-US}}</ref> were introduced, and more films were made in color—which soon became the rule, rather than the exception. Some important mainstream Hollywood films were still being made in black-and-white as late as the mid-1960s, but they marked the end of an era.<ref name=":16" /> Color television receivers had been available in the U.S. since the mid-1950s, but initially, they were very expensive and few broadcasts were in [[color]].<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |date=2014-01-06 |title=The decline of black and white TV {{!}} National Science and Media Museum |url=https://blog.scienceandmediamuseum.org.uk/the-decline-of-black-and-white-tv/ |access-date=2025-07-15 |website=National Science and Media Museum blog |language=en-GB}}</ref>

During the 1960s, prices gradually came down, color broadcasts became common,<ref name=":17" /> and sales boomed. The overwhelming public verdict in favor of color was clear. After the final flurry of black-and-white films had been released in mid-decade, all Hollywood studio productions were filmed in color,<ref name=":16" /> with the usual exceptions made only at the insistence of "star" [[Filmmaking|filmmakers]] such as [[Peter Bogdanovich]], [[Martin Scorsese]], and [[Alfred Hitchcock]] with his film ''[[Psycho (1960 film)|Psycho]]'' (1960).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilkinson |first=Alissa |date=2021-11-09 |title=Why are all the movies in black and white? |url=https://www.vox.com/22745191/black-white-movies-belfast-passing-cmon |access-date=2025-07-15 |website=Vox |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== 1960s–present: Modern cinema ===

[[File:Salahzulfikar1.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Salah Zulfikar]], one of the most popular actors in the golden age of [[Cinema of Egypt|Egyptian Cinema]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Kijamii|title=11 Golden Age Egyptian Actors We Still Have A Crush On Today {{!}} NileFM {{!}} EGYPT'S#1 FOR HIT MUSIC|url=https://nilefm.com/entertainment/article/357/ten-egyptian-hot-male-celebrities-that-our-moms-still-have-a-crush-on|access-date=2021-10-01|website=nilefm.com|archive-date=14 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211114210230/https://nilefm.com/entertainment/article/357/ten-egyptian-hot-male-celebrities-that-our-moms-still-have-a-crush-on|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Remembering Salah Zulficar - Film - Arts & Culture |url=https://english.ahram.org.eg/News/2408.aspx |access-date=2025-09-08 |website=Ahram Online}}</ref>]]

The decades following the decline of the [[studio system]] in the 1960s saw changes in the production and style of film. Various "New Wave" movements (including the [[French New Wave]], [[New German Cinema]] wave, [[Parallel Cinema|Indian New Wave]], [[Japanese New Wave]], [[New Hollywood]], and [[Cinema of Egypt|Egyptian New Wave]])<ref>{{Cite book |last=Martin |first=Sean |url=http://archive.org/details/newwavesincinema0000mart |title=New waves in cinema |date=2013 |publisher=Harpenden : Kamera Books |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-1-84243-447-5}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Brookman |first=Luke |date=2017-11-14 |title=The 10 Greatest New Wave Movements in Film History |url=https://www.tasteofcinema.com/2017/the-10-greatest-new-wave-movements-in-film-history/2/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=Taste of Cinema - Movie Reviews and Classic Movie Lists |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=TCM Spotlight: New Waves Around the World |url=https://www.tcm.com/articles/021460/tcm-spotlight-new-waves-around-the-world |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=Turner Classic Movies |language=en-us}}</ref> and the rise of film-school-educated independent filmmakers,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Banks |first=Miranda |date=2019-06-03 |title=Film Schools as Pre-Industry: Fostering Creative Collaboration and Equity in Media Production Programs |url=https://quod.lib.umich.edu/m/mij/15031809.0006.105/--film-schools-as-pre-industry-fostering-creative?rgn=main;view=fulltext |journal=Media Industries Journal |language=en |volume=6 |issue=1 |doi=10.3998/mij.15031809.0006.105 |issn=2373-9037 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240723111534/https://quod.lib.umich.edu/m/mij/15031809.0006.105/--film-schools-as-pre-industry-fostering-creative?rgn=main;view=fulltext |archive-date=2024-07-23|hdl=2027/spo.15031809.0006.105 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=O'Conor |first=Kerry |date=2017-07-05 |title=The Evolution of Film School in America: Everything to Know, From Dropouts to Disciples, Fairbanks to Francis Ford - MovieMaker Magazine |url=https://www.moviemaker.com/evolution-of-film-school-in-america-everything-to-know-fairbanks-francis-ford/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |language=en-US}}</ref> known as the "Film School Generation" of the 1960s and 1970s,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Doll |first=Susan |date=2018-06-14 |title=The All-American Boy |url=https://www.tcm.com/articles/1414368/the-all-american-boy |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=Turner Classic Movies |language=en-us}}</ref> contributed to the changes the medium experienced in the latter half of the 20th century.

[[Digital cinematography|Digital technology]] has been the driving force for change throughout the 1990s and into the 2000s. Digital [[3D viewer|3D projection]] largely replaced earlier problem-prone 3D film systems of the 1950s<ref name=":18">{{Cite web |last=Wakeman |first=Gregory |date=2025-12-22 |title=Why America Fell in Love With 3D Movies |url=https://www.history.com/articles/3d-movies-theaters-tech-timeline-rise-fall |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=HISTORY |language=en}}</ref> and 1980s<ref>{{Cite web |last=Goldberg |first=Matt |date=2018-04-06 |title=3D Movies Are Dead Again |url=https://collider.com/3d-movies-are-dead-again/ |access-date=2025-07-13 |website=Collider |language=en}}</ref> and became briefly popular in the early 2010s with films like ''[[Avatar (2009 film)|Avatar]]'' (2009).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2010-02-05 |title=The 3D Renaissance |url=https://www.projectorcentral.com/3d_projectors_technology.htm |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=www.projectorcentral.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":18" /> Large-screen cinemas systems using [[35 mm movie film|35mm]] and [[70 mm film|70mm film]] were developed in the late 2010s, with companies like the [[IMAX Corporation|IMAX corporation]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=A very short history of cinema {{!}} National Science and Media Museum |url=https://www.scienceandmediamuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/very-short-history-of-cinema |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250605162447/https://www.scienceandmediamuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/very-short-history-of-cinema |archive-date=2025-06-05 |access-date=2025-07-13 |website=National Science and Media Museum |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> By the mid-2010s, theatres were also trying a [[4D film|4D]] approach to movies, in which audiences could experience smells, wind, smoke/fog, vibrations, and other sensations.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Barnes |first=Brooks |date=2014-11-29 |title=To Lure Young, Movie Theaters Shake, Smell and Spritz |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/11/30/business/media/to-lure-young-movie-theaters-shake-smell-and-spritz.html |access-date=2026-07-06 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=4-D Films {{!}} Museum of Science |url=https://www.mos.org/visit/4-D |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=www.mos.org |language=en}}</ref> By the mid-2020s, an even more "immersive" [[4DX]] film format was gaining popularity.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shanfeld |first=Ethan |date=2024-08-15 |title=With 'Twisters,' 4DX Finally Swept America. Where Does Hollywood Go From Here? |url=https://variety.com/2024/film/news/twisters-4dx-water-wind-seats-1236105586/ |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=Variety |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Film theory ==
[[File:BolexH16.jpg|thumb|left|alt=16 mm spring-wound Bolex H16 Reflex camera|This [[16 mm film|16 mm]] spring-wound [[Bolex]] "H16" Reflex camera is a popular entry level camera used in [[film school]]s.]]

"[[Film theory]]" seeks to develop concise and systematic concepts or principles that apply to the study of film as [[art]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hall |first=Lucinda M. |title=Research Guides: Film Studies: Film theory |url=https://researchguides.dartmouth.edu/filmstudies/filmtheory |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=researchguides.dartmouth.edu |language=en}}</ref> The concept of film as an art-form began in 1911 with [[Ricciotto Canudo]]'s manifest ''The Birth of the Sixth Art''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ACT. Shorts in the Museum - Gregory Allicar Museum of Art {{!}} Colorado State University |url=https://artmuseum.colostate.edu/programs/act-shorts-in-the-museum/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=artmuseum.colostate.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Merjian |first=Ara H. |date=2008-01-01 |title=A Screen for Projection: Ricciotto Canudo's Exponential Aesthetics and the Parisian Avant-gardes |url=https://www.academia.edu/37967406 |journal=European Film Theory}}</ref> The [[Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography|Moscow Film School]], the oldest film school in the world, was founded in 1919, to teach about and research film theory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography |url=https://www.topuniversities.com/universities/gerasimov-institute-cinematography |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Top Universities |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Moscow Film School |url=https://www.creme.ac.th/moscow-film-school/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Crème Academy |language=en-GB}}</ref> [[Formalist film theory]], led by [[Rudolf Arnheim]], [[Béla Balázs]], and [[Siegfried Kracauer]], emphasized how film differed from reality and thus could be considered a valid [[fine art]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Introduction: Film Theory, Cinema, the Body, and the Senses |url=https://elsaesser.dff.film/archive/introduction-film-theory-cinema-the-body-and-the-senses |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Thomas Elsaesser Collection}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Moltke |first=Johannes von |date=2013 |title=Theory of the Novel: The Literary Imagination of Classical Film Theory |url=https://www.academia.edu/4715403 |journal=October Magazine, LTD. And Massachusetts Institute of Technology |via=Academia}}</ref> [[André Bazin]] reacted against this theory by arguing that film's artistic essence lay in its ability to mechanically reproduce reality, not in its differences from reality, and this gave rise to [[Realism (arts)#Cinema|realist theory]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-04-18 |title=Divining the real: the leaps of faith in André Bazin's film criticism |url=https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/features/divining-real-leaps-faith-andre-bazins-film-criticism |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=BFI |language=en|last=Matthews|first=Peter}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Blokh |first=Danya |date=2022-12-04 |title=Between Realism and Imagination |url=https://yale-herald.com/2022/12/04/between-realism-and-imagination/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=The Yale Herald |language=en-US}}</ref> More recent analysis spurred by [[Jacques Lacan]]'s psychoanalysis,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jacques Lacan in Film and Media Theory |url=https://fiveable.me/film-and-media-theory/key-terms/jacques-lacan |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=fiveable.me |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tilakaratne |first=Wishka |date=2022-06-17 |title=Lacanian Film Theory: A Very Brief Introduction |url=https://movieweb.com/lacanian-film-theory-a-brief-introduction/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=MovieWeb |language=en}}</ref> [[Ferdinand de Saussure]]'s [[semiotics]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ferdinand de Saussure {{!}} Intro to Film Theory |url=https://fiveable.me/introduction-to-film-theory/key-terms/ferdinand-de-saussure |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=fiveable.me |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Alsberry |first=Kyle |date=2024-05-15 |title=Ferdinand de Saussure: The linguist who unexpectedly helped create film theory |url=https://www.videomaker.com/how-to/directing/film-history/ferdinand-de-saussure-the-linguist-who-unexpectedly-helped-create-film-theory/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Videomaker |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Laura Mulvey]]'s [[male gaze]] theory,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sampson |first=Rachael |date=2015-10-27 |title=Film Theory 101 - Laura Mulvey: The Male Gaze Theory |url=https://www.filminquiry.com/film-theory-basics-laura-mulvey-male-gaze-theory/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Film Inquiry |language=en-US}}</ref> among others, has given rise to [[psychoanalytic film theory]],<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2014-06-07 |title=Psychological Film Theory |url=https://www.filmtheory.org/psychological-film-theory/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Film Theory |language=en-US}}</ref> [[structuralist film theory]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lybarger |first=Lowell |title=Research Guides Home: Semiotics: Saussure |url=https://libguides.atu.edu/c.php?g=1481744&p=11044218 |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=libguides.atu.edu |language=en}}</ref> [[feminist film theory]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stecher |first=Gabrielle |date=2023-09-11 |title=Feminist Film Theory: An Introductory Reading List |url=https://daily.jstor.org/feminist-film-theory-an-introductory-reading-list/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=JSTOR Daily |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hall |first=Lucinda M. |title=Research Guides: Film Studies: Feminist film theory |url=https://researchguides.dartmouth.edu/filmstudies/feministfilmtheory |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=researchguides.dartmouth.edu |language=en}}</ref> and others. On the other hand, critics from the [[analytical philosophy]] tradition, influenced by [[Wittgenstein|Ludwig Wittgenstein]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mambrol |first=Nasrullah |date=2019-04-21 |title=Key Theories of Ludwig Wittgenstein |url=https://literariness.org/2019/04/21/key-theories-of-ludwig-wittgenstein/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Literary Theory and Criticism |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Biletzki |first1=Anat |title=Ludwig Wittgenstein |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2023/entries/wittgenstein/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |edition=Fall 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Matar |first2=Anat |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref> try to clarify misconceptions used in theoretical studies and produce analysis of a film's vocabulary and its link to a [[form of life]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Klevan |first=Andrew |date=2020-01-01 |title=ORDINARY LANGUAGE FILM STUDIES ANDREW KLEVAN ACADEMIA EDU VERSION |url=https://www.academia.edu/43723219 |journal=Aesthetic Investigations |doi=10.58519/aesthinv.v3i2.11945 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Horwich |first=Paul |date=2013-03-04 |title=Was Wittgenstein Right? |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/03/03/was-wittgenstein-right/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Opinionator |language=en}}</ref>

=== Language ===
Film is considered to have its own [[language]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-03-17 |title=The Language of Film: Definition, Theories, Key Thinkers, and Indian Perspectives |url=https://literarylatitude.com/2025/03/17/the-language-of-film-definition-theories-key-thinkers-and-indian-perspectives/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Literary Latitude |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Film Education {{!}} Topics {{!}} Storytelling on film {{!}} Film language |url=https://www.filmeducation.org/resources/primary/topics/storytelling_on_film/film_language/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=www.filmeducation.org |language=en}}</ref> [[James Monaco]] wrote a classic text on film theory, titled "''How to Read a Film''," that addresses this.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Monaco |first=James |title=How to read a film: movies, media, and beyond art, technology, language, history, theory |date=2009 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-532105-0 |edition=Fourth edition, completely revised and expanded |location=Oxford New York}}</ref> Director [[Ingmar Bergman]] famously said, "[[Andrei Tarkovsky]] for me is the greatest [[Film director|director]], the one who invented a ''new language'', true to the nature of film, as it captures life as a reflection, life as a dream."<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-10-22 |title=10 great films that inspired Andrei Tarkovsky |url=https://www.bfi.org.uk/lists/10-great-films-inspired-andrei-tarkovsky |access-date=2026-04-17 |website=BFI |language=en}}</ref> 

An example of film language is a "[[shot/reverse shot]]" or a sequence of back and forth images of a character looking [[offscreen]], followed by another character, then a repetition of this, which is a language understood by the audience to indicate a conversation or other type of interaction.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2021-07-16 |title=Shot/Reverse Shot |url=https://www.filmmakersacademy.com/glossary/shot-reverse-shot/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Filmmakers Academy |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-28 |title=What Is a Shot/Reverse Shot? How to Film Conversations |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/what-is-shot-reverse-shot-film-examples-75550/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref> This describes another theory of film, the [[180-degree rule]], as a visual story-telling device with an ability to place a viewer in a context of being psychologically present through the use of visual composition and editing.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Academy |first=Filmmakers |date=2026-05-12 |title=Filmmakers Academy Premium Education |url=https://www.filmmakersacademy.com/blog-camera-180-degree-rule/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Filmmakers Academy |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=University |first=Columbia |title=Columbia Film Language Glossary: 180-Degree Rule |url=https://filmglossary.ccnmtl.columbia.edu/term/180-degree-rule/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=filmglossary.ccnmtl.columbia.edu |language=en}}</ref> The "[[Classical Hollywood cinema|Hollywood style]]" includes this narrative theory, due to the overwhelming practice of the rule by movie studios based in Hollywood, California, during film's classical era.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Classic Hollywood Narrative Style |url=http://history.sandiego.edu/gen/filmnotes/classical.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030318060806/http://history.sandiego.edu/gen/filmnotes/classical.html |archive-date=2003-03-18 |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=history.sandiego.edu}}</ref> Another example of cinematic language is having a shot that zooms in on an actor with an expression of reflection that cuts to a shot of a younger actor who vaguely resembles the first actor, indicating that the character is remembering a past self. Known as a "[[Flashback (narrative)#Film|flashback]]," it is an edit of compositions that causes a time transition and typically reveals information about the character's history to the audience.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Reeves |first=Nate |date=2022-02-17 |title=The 10 Best Flashbacks In Movies, Ranked |url=https://www.cbr.com/best-flashbacks-in-movies/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=CBR |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Walkley |first=Luke |date=2022-04-14 |title=6 Powerful Uses of Flashback Scenes in Film |url=https://www.moviemarker.co.uk/6-powerful-uses-of-flashback-scenes-in-film/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Movie Marker |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Montage ===
{{Main|Montage (filmmaking)}}

[[Montage (filmmaking)|Montage]] is a film editing technique in which separate pieces of film are selected, edited, and assembled to create a new section or sequence within a film. This technique can be used to convey a narrative or to create an emotional or intellectual effect by juxtaposing different shots, often for the purpose of condensing time, space, or information. Montage can involve [[Flashback (psychology)|flashbacks]], parallel action, or the interplay of various visual elements to enhance the storytelling or create [[symbolic meaning]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sealy |first1=Peter |title=Review: Montage and the Metropolis: Architecture, Modernity, and the Representation of Space, by Martino Stierli |journal=Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians |date=September 2019 |volume=78 |issue=3 |pages=364–367 |doi=10.1525/jsah.2019.78.3.364 }}</ref>

The concept of montage emerged in the 1920s, with pioneering Soviet filmmakers like [[Sergei Eisenstein]] and [[Lev Kuleshov]] developing the theory of montage. Eisenstein's film ''[[Battleship Potemkin]]'' (1925) is an example of the innovative use of montage, where he employed complex [[juxtaposition]]s of images to create a visceral impact on the audience.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ball |first=E |date=2018 |title=Sergei Eisenstein's Montage: Film Editing and the Theory of Attractions |journal=JSTOR Daily}}{{verify source|date=January 2026}}</ref>

As the art of montage evolved, filmmakers began incorporating musical and visual counterpoint to create more dynamic and engaging experiences for viewers. The development of scene construction through [[mise-en-scène]], editing, and [[special effect]]s led to more sophisticated techniques that can be compared to those utilized in opera and ballet.<ref name=FilmEditing>{{Cite web |title=Film editing {{!}} motion pictures {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/art/film-editing |access-date=2023-03-25 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref>

The [[French New Wave]] movement of the late 1950s and 1960s also embraced the montage technique, with filmmakers such as [[Jean-Luc Godard]] and [[François Truffaut]] using montage to create distinct and innovative films.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Wave {{!}} French film style {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/art/New-Wave-film |access-date=2023-03-25 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref>

In contemporary cinema, montage continues to play a role in shaping narratives and creating emotional, memorable sequences. Filmmakers have adapted the traditional montage technique to suit the evolving aesthetics and storytelling styles of modern cinema.<ref name=":19">{{Cite web |last=Hellerman |first=Jason |date=2024-09-16 |title=What Is a Montage in Film and Television? |url=https://nofilmschool.com/what-is-a-montage |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=No Film School |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":20">{{Cite web |last=Gates |first=Chris Ace |date=2015-10-07 |title=What is a montage? The Soviet Montage Theory explained |url=https://www.videomaker.com/article/c1/18352-soviet-montage-theory-everything-old-is-new-again/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Videomaker |language=en-US}}</ref>

* Rapid editing and fast-paced montages: With the advent of digital editing tools, filmmakers can create rapid and intricate montages to convey information or emotions quickly. Films like [[Darren Aronofsky]]'s ''[[Requiem for a Dream]]'' (2000) and [[Edgar Wright]]'s ''[[Shaun of the Dead]]'' (2004) employ fast-paced editing techniques to create immersive and intense experiences for the audience.<ref name="FilmEditing" />
* Music video influence: The influence of music videos on film has led to the incorporation of stylized montage sequences, often accompanied by popular music. Films like ''[[Guardians of the Galaxy (film)|Guardians of the Galaxy]]'' (2014) and ''[[Baby Driver]]'' (2017) use montage to create visually striking sequences that are both entertaining and narratively functional.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-07-25 |title=Read This: It's okay to hate John McCain's legacy |url=https://www.avclub.com/read-this-it-s-okay-to-hate-john-mccain-s-legacy-1798264356 |access-date=2023-03-25 |website=The A.V. Club |language=en}}</ref>
* Sports and training montages: The sports and training montage has become a staple in modern cinema, often used to condense time and show a character's growth or development. Examples can be found in films like ''[[Rocky]]'' (1976), ''[[The Karate Kid]]'' (1984), and ''[[Million Dollar Baby]]'' (2004).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Desser |first=D. |date=2018 |title=Sports Film |url=https://www.britannica.com/art/sports-film}}</ref>
* Cross-cutting and parallel action: Contemporary filmmakers use montage to create tension and suspense by [[cross-cutting]] between parallel storylines. [[Christopher Nolan filmography|Christopher Nolan's]] ''[[Inception]]'' (2010) and ''[[Dunkirk (2017 film)|Dunkirk]]'' (2017) employ complex cross-cutting techniques to build narrative momentum and heighten the audience's emotional engagement.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Abrams |first=S. |date=2017 |title=How Christopher Nolan's 'Dunkirk' Is Like a Silent Film |work=The Hollywood Reporter}}</ref>
* Thematic montage: Montage can also be used to convey thematic elements or [[Motifs in mythology|motifs]] in a film. [[Wes Anderson filmography|Wes Anderson's]] ''[[The Royal Tenenbaums]]'' (2001) employs montage to create a visual language that reflects the film's [[Theme (narrative)|themes]] of family, nostalgia, and loss.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wes Anderson {{!}} Biography, Movies, & Facts {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Wes-Anderson |access-date=2023-03-25 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref>

As the medium of film continues to evolve, montage remains an integral aspect of visual storytelling, with filmmakers finding new and innovative ways to employ this technique.<ref name=":19" /><ref name=":20" />

=== Film criticism ===
{{Main|Film criticism}}

[[File:Russ Meyer and Roger Ebert by Roger Ebert.jpg|thumb|Chicago critic [[Roger Ebert]] (right) with director [[Russ Meyer]]]]

Film criticism is the analysis and evaluation of films.<ref name=":21">{{Cite web |last=Mardeusz |first=Patricia |title=UVM Libraries Research Guides: Film & Television Studies: Reviews vs Criticism |url=https://researchguides.uvm.edu/c.php?g=290200&p=3481769 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171006191319/https://researchguides.uvm.edu/c.php?g=290200&p=3481769 |archive-date=2017-10-06 |access-date=2025-11-13 |website=researchguides.uvm.edu |language=en}}</ref> Traditionally, this was divided into two categories:<ref name=":23" /> 

* Academic criticism by [[Film studies|film scholars]]: Critics who take a more academic approach to films, through publishing in film journals and writing books about films using [[film theory]] or [[film studies]] approaches, study how film and filming techniques work, and what effect they have on people. Rather than having their reviews published in newspapers or appearing on television, their articles are published in scholarly journals or up-market magazines. They also tend to be affiliated with colleges or universities as professors or instructors.<ref name=":21" />
* Journalistic film criticism: Journalist film critics are sometimes called film reviewers.<ref name=":21" /> Film critics working for [[newspaper]]s, [[magazine]]s, and [[broadcast media]]<ref name=":23">{{Cite web |last=Howard |first=Jessica |title=Research Guides: Criticism: Literature, Film & Drama: Film Criticism |url=https://libguides.dickinson.edu/criticism/film |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=libguides.dickinson.edu |language=en}}</ref> mainly review new releases and tend to be more "consumer-oriented".<ref name=":21" />

With the advent of online [[Review aggregator|review aggregators]], like [[Metacritic]] and [[Rotten Tomatoes]],{{cn|date=July 2026}} reviews from both critics and audiences have become easily accessible. A high or low score on a review aggregator can help drive or deter viewers from going to theatres, despite persuasive [[movie marketing]]. Similarly, [[Word-of-mouth marketing|word-of-mouth]] buzz and audience reviews via social media can impact enthusiasm for a film.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Teasdale |first=Aaron |date=2024-09-03 |title=Film industry realities: reviews and box office impact |url=https://www.meer.com/en/80240-film-industry-realities-reviews-and-box-office-impact |access-date=2026-07-08 |website=Meer |language=en}}</ref> 

{{quote box
| quoted = 1|If a movie can illuminate the lives of other people who share this planet with us and show us not only how different they are but, how even so, they share the same dreams and hurts, then it deserves to be called great.
| source = — [[Roger Ebert]] (1986)<ref>{{Cite news|last=Ebert|first=Roger|date=October 25, 1986|url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/A-love-story-forged-in-hell|title=Sid and Nancy|newspaper=[[Chicago Sun-Times]]|access-date=May 31, 2020|via=[[RogerEbert.com]]|archive-date=April 5, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200405191646/https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/A-love-story-forged-in-hell|url-status=live}}</ref>
| width = 25%
| align = right
| style = padding:8px;
| border = 1px
}}The impact of a reviewer on a given film's [[box office]] performance is a matter of debate.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chiu |first1=Ya-Ling |last2=Du |first2=Jiangze |last3=Sun |first3=Yide |last4=Wang |first4=Jying-Nan |date=2022 |title=Do Critical Reviews Affect Box Office Revenues Through Community Engagement and User Reviews? |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |volume=13 |article-number=900360 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2022.900360 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-1078 |pmc=9204591 |pmid=35719485}}</ref> For example, positive film reviews have been shown to spark interest in little-known films.<ref name=":22">{{Cite web |date=2004-10-26 |title=Do film critics still matter? |url=https://www.today.com/popculture/do-film-critics-still-matter-wbna6338400 |access-date=2026-07-08 |website=TODAY.com |language=en}}</ref> Conversely, mass marketed [[action film|action]] and [[comedy film]]s tend not to be greatly affected by a critic's overall judgment of a film; similarly, [[Horror film|horror]] and [[Science fiction film|sci-fi]] fans generally see anything in their genre, regardless of reviews.<ref name=":22" /> In 2004, a survey found that TV ads and recommendations from others had the most influence on movie-going habits, with each factor cited by about 70% of respondents. Professional reviews ran at 33%, while online ratings influenced 28%.<ref name=":22" /> However, there have been many films in which film companies had so little confidence in a project that they refused to give reviewers an advanced viewing (or "pre-screening") to avoid widespread panning of the film.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Lee |date=2020-04-18 |title=10 Movies Not Screened For Critics (That Were Actually Good) |url=https://whatculture.com/film/10-movies-not-screened-for-critics-that-were-actually-good |access-date=2026-07-12 |website=WhatCulture.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Singer |first=Matt SingerMatt |date=2020-09-10 |title=Movies That Weren’t Screened For Critics That Were Actually Good |url=https://screencrush.com/movies-that-werent-screened-for-critics-that-were-actually-good/ |access-date=2026-07-12 |website=ScreenCrush |language=en}}</ref>
== Industry ==
{{World Cinema}}
{{Main|Film industry}}

The making and showing of motion pictures became a source of profit almost as soon as the process was invented. Upon seeing how successful their new invention, and its product, was in their native France, the [[Auguste and Louis Lumière|Lumière brothers]] set about touring the continent to exhibit the first films at public screenings. They opened Cinématographe theaters in London, Brussels, and Belgium.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pruitt |first=Sarah |date=2014-10-03 |title=The Lumière Brothers, Pioneers of Cinema |url=https://www.history.com/articles/the-lumiere-brothers-pioneers-of-cinema |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=HISTORY |language=en}}</ref> 

April 1896 is considered the birth of the American movie theater, with [[Thomas Edison|Edison]] renting the [[Koster & Bial's Music Hall|Koster and Bial’s Music Hall]] for the first public demonstration of his Vitascope after he learned the Lumieres were planning their first American exhibition.<ref name=":24">{{Cite web |last=Roos |first=Dave |date=2025-02-27 |title=How Movie Theaters Got Their Start in America |url=https://www.history.com/articles/movie-theaters-origins-america |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=HISTORY |language=en}}</ref> 

[[File:Filmstudio Babelsberg Eingang.jpg|thumb|alt=Babelsberg Studio near Berlin gate with pedestrian island|Founded in 1912, the [[Babelsberg Studio]] near [[Berlin]] was the first large-scale film studio in the world, and the forerunner to [[Hollywood, Los Angeles|Hollywood]]. It still produces global blockbusters every year.|left]]The [[Oberammergau Passion Play]] of 1898<ref>{{Cite book|last=Couvares|first=Francis G.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=D5R7NNAuH1AC&dq=Oberammergau+Passion+Play+1898&pg=PA63|title=Movie Censorship and American Culture|date=2006|publisher=Univ of Massachusetts Press|isbn=978-1-55849-575-3|language=en|access-date=2022-01-17|archive-date=2022-03-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220311110351/https://books.google.com/books?id=D5R7NNAuH1AC&dq=Oberammergau+Passion+Play+1898&pg=PA63|url-status=live}}</ref> was the first commercial motion picture ever produced. Other pictures soon followed, and motion pictures became a separate industry that overshadowed [[vaudeville]].<ref name=":24" /> Dedicated [[movie theater|theaters]] and companies formed specifically to produce and distribute films,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pickford |first=Mary |title=The Business of Movies |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/pickford-business-movies/ |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=PBS |language=en}}</ref> while motion picture actors became major [[celebrity|celebrities]] and commanded huge fees for their performances. By 1917, [[Charlie Chaplin]] had a contract that called for an annual salary of $1 million for eight films.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rozenberg |first=Hailey |date=2020-04-21 |title=Charlie Chaplin Biographical Timeline |url=https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/charlie-chaplin-biographical-timeline/14049/ |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=PBS |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-01-15 |title=It's Mutual: Charlie Chaplin Shorts, 1916–1917 |url=https://silentfilm.org/its-mutual-charlie-chaplin-shorts-1916-1917/ |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=San Francisco Silent Film Festival |language=en-US}}</ref> From 1931 to 1956, film was also the only image storage and playback system for [[television programming]]<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UdwDAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA227&lpg=PA227&#v=onepage&q&f=false |title=Popular Mechanics |date=April 1953 |publisher=Hearst Magazines |year=1953 |pages=227 |language=en}}</ref> until the introduction of [[videotape recorder]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-17 |title=Milestones:Ampex Videotape Recorder, 1956 |url=https://ethw.org/Milestones:Ampex_Videotape_Recorder,_1956 |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=ETHW |language=en}}</ref>

In the U.S., much of the film industry is centered around [[Hollywood, California]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roland |first=Zelda |date=2017-11-07 |title=How Did Hollywood End Up in...Hollywood? |url=https://www.pbssocal.org/shows/lost-la/how-did-hollywood-end-up-in-hollywood |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=PBS SoCal |language=en}}</ref> Other regional centers exist in many parts of the world, such as [[Mumbai]]-centered [[Bollywood]], the [[Cinema of India|Indian film industry's]] [[Hindi]] cinema that produces the largest number of films in the world.<ref>[https://www.cnn.com/2004/WORLD/asiapcf/04/07/india.sexywood/index.html Bollywood Hots Up] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080307024113/https://www.cnn.com/2004/WORLD/asiapcf/04/07/india.sexywood/index.html |date=2008-03-07 }} cnn.com. Retrieved June 23, 2007.</ref> Though the expense involved in making films has led cinema production to concentrate under the auspices of [[movie studio]]s,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024 |title=Hollywoodland: The Origins of the Studios |url=https://www.academymuseum.org/programs/series/hollywoodland-the-origins-of-the-studios |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=Academy Museum of Motion Pictures |language=en}}</ref> recent advances in affordable film making equipment have allowed independent film productions to flourish.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-17 |title=How technology has changed the film industry |url=https://www.falmouth.ac.uk/news/how-technology-has-changed-film-industry |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=www.falmouth.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref>[[File:Misr Studio old.jpg|thumb|Founded in 1935, [[Studio Misr]] near the [[Giza pyramid complex|Giza Pyramid complex]], was the first large-scale film studio in [[Africa]] and the [[Middle East]].]]

Profit is a key force in the industry, due to the costly and risky nature of filmmaking; many films have large [[cost overruns]], an example being [[Kevin Costner]]'s ''[[Waterworld]]''. Yet many filmmakers strive to create works of lasting social significance. The [[Academy Awards]] (also known as "the Oscars") are the most prominent film awards in the United States, providing recognition each year to films, based on their artistic merits. There is also a large industry for educational and instructional films made in lieu of or in addition to lectures and texts. Revenue in the industry is sometimes volatile due to the reliance on [[blockbuster film]]s released in [[movie theater]]s. The rise of alternative home entertainment has raised questions about the future of the cinema industry, and Hollywood employment has become less reliable, particularly for medium and low-budget films.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Christopherson |first1=S. |title=Hollywood in decline? US film and television producers beyond the era of fiscal crisis |journal=Cambridge Journal of Regions, Economy and Society |date=March 2013 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=141–157 |doi=10.1093/cjres/rss024 }}</ref>

== Associated fields ==
{{Further|Film theory|Product placement|Propaganda}}

Derivative academic fields of study may both interact with and develop independently of filmmaking, as in [[film theory]] and analysis. Fields of academic study have been created that are derivative or dependent on the existence of film, such as [[film criticism]], [[film history]], divisions of [[film propaganda]] in authoritarian governments, or psychological on subliminal effects (e.g., of a flashing soda can during a screening). These fields may further create derivative fields, such as a [[movie review]] section in a newspaper or a television guide. Sub-industries can spin off from film, such as popcorn makers, and film-related toys (e.g., [[Star Wars action figures|''Star Wars'' figures]]). Sub-industries of pre-existing industries may deal specifically with film, such as [[product placement]] and other [[advertising]] within films.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

== Terminology ==
The terminology used for describing motion pictures varies considerably between [[British and American English]]. In British usage, the name of the medium is ''film''. The word ''movie'' is understood but seldom used.<ref name="britam">{{Cite web|title=British English/American English Vocabulary|url=https://www.englishclub.com/vocabulary/british-american.htm|access-date=26 June 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130621191145/https://www.englishclub.com/vocabulary/british-american.htm|archive-date=21 June 2013}}</ref><ref name="sdope">{{Cite web|title=British English vs. U.S. English – film vs. movie|url=https://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=363802|work=Straight Dope Message Board|date = 21 March 2006|access-date=26 June 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140110091840/https://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=363802|archive-date=10 January 2014}}</ref> Additionally, ''the pictures'' (plural) is used somewhat frequently to refer to the place where movies are exhibited; in American English this may be called ''the movies'', but that term is becoming outdated. In other countries, the place where movies are exhibited may be called a ''cinema'' or ''[[movie theatre]]''.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

By contrast, in the United States, ''movie'' is the predominant term for the medium. Although the words ''film'' and ''movie'' are sometimes used interchangeably, ''film'' is more often used when considering a work's [[artistic]], [[theoretical]], or [[technology|technical]] aspects. The term ''movie'' more often refers to a work's [[entertainment]] or [[Commerce|commercial]] aspects.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

Further terminology is used to distinguish various forms and media used in the film industry. ''Motion pictures'' and ''moving pictures'' are frequently used terms for films and movie productions specifically intended for theatrical exhibitions, such as ''[[Star Wars (film)|Star Wars]]'', although in [[United States copyright law]], the term ''motion picture'' refers to any work consisting of moving images regardless of format or length.<ref name="comp800">{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://www.copyright.gov/comp3/chap800/ch800-performing-arts.pdf|chapter=Chapter 800: Works of the Performing Arts|title=[[Compendium of U.S. Copyright Office Practices]]|publisher=[[United States Copyright Office]]|date=2021-01-28|access-date=2025-09-07 |quote=Motion pictures include movies of all genres (e.g., action, drama, horror, comedy, animation, documentary, etc.), regardless of whether the movie is intended for release in theaters, on television, on DVD or other video format, or online. Other examples include [[television program]]s and [[Television advertisement|commercials]] (e.g., comedy, drama, reality, news, advertisements), [[Music video|music]] and [[Educational film|educational videos]], and [[Short-form content|short videos]] posted online. |page=99}}</ref> ''[[DVD]]'', ''[[Blu-ray Disc]]'', and ''[[videotape]]'' are video formats that can reproduce a photochemical film. A reproduction based on such is called a ''transfer''. After the advent of theatrical film as an industry, the television industry began using videotape as a recording medium. For many decades, tape was solely an analog medium onto which moving images could be either recorded or transferred. ''Film'' and ''filming'' refer to the photochemical medium that chemically records a visual image and the act of recording respectively. However, the act of shooting images with other visual media, such as with a digital camera, is still called ''filming'', and the resulting works often called ''films'' as interchangeable to ''movies'', despite not being shot on film. ''[[Silent films]]'' need not be utterly silent, but are films and movies without an audible dialogue, including those that have a musical accompaniment. The word ''[[talkies]]'' refers to the earliest sound films created to have [[Hearing (sense)|audible]] [[dialogue]] recorded for playback along with the film, regardless of a musical accompaniment. ''Cinema'' either broadly encompasses both films and movies, or it is roughly synonymous with film and theatrical exhibition, and both are capitalized when referring to a category of art. The ''[[silver screen]]'' refers to the projection screen used to exhibit films and, by extension, is also used as a [[metonym]] for the entire film industry.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

''[[Widescreen]]'' refers to a larger width to height in the [[film frame|frame]], compared to earlier historic [[aspect ratio (image)|aspect ratios]].<ref name="imdbmovietermsw">{{Cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/glossary/W |title=Movie Terminology Glossary: W |publisher=[[IMDb]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100722052010/https://www.imdb.com/glossary/W |archive-date=2010-07-22 }}</ref> A ''feature-length film'', or ''[[feature film]]'', is of a conventional full length, usually 60 minutes or more, and can commercially stand by itself without other films in a ticketed screening.<ref name="imdbmovietermsf">{{Cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/glossary/F |title=Movie Terminology Glossary: F |publisher=[[IMDb]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100722051945/https://www.imdb.com/glossary/F |archive-date=2010-07-22 }}</ref> A ''[[short subject|short]]'' is a film that is not as long as a feature-length film, often screened with other shorts, or preceding a feature-length film. An ''[[Independent film|independent]]'' is a film made outside the conventional film industry.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

In American usage, one talks of a ''[[Film screening|screening]]'' or ''[[Movie projector|projection]]'' of a movie or video on a [[Projection screen|screen]] at a public or private ''theater''. In British English, a ''film showing'' happens at a ''[[movie theatre|cinema]]'' (never a ''[[theatre]]'', which is a different medium and place altogether).<ref name="sdope" /> ''Cinema'' usually refers to an arena designed specifically to exhibit films, where the screen is affixed to a wall, while ''theatre'' usually refers to a place where live, non-recorded action or combination thereof occurs from a podium or other type of stage, including the amphitheatre. Theatres can still screen movies in them, though the theatre would be retrofitted to do so. One might propose ''going to the cinema'' when referring to the activity, or sometimes ''to the pictures'' in British English, whereas the American expression is usually ''going to the movies''. A cinema usually shows a mass-marketed movie using a front-projection screen process with either a film projector or, more recently, with a digital projector. But cinemas may also show theatrical movies from their home video transfers that include Blu-ray Disc, DVD, and videocassette when they possess sufficient projection quality or based upon need, such as movies that exist only in their transferred state, which may be due to the loss or deterioration of the film master and prints from which the movie originally existed. Due to the advent of [[digital cinema|digital film production and distribution]], physical film might be absent entirely.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

A ''[[double feature]]'' is a screening of two independently marketed, stand-alone feature films. A ''viewing'' is a watching of a film. ''[[Sales]]'' and ''at the box office'' refer to tickets sold at a theater, or more currently, rights sold for individual showings. A ''[[Film release|release]]'' is the distribution and often simultaneous screening of a film. A ''[[preview (theatre)|preview]]'' is a screening in advance of the main release.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

Any film may also have a ''[[sequel]]'', which portrays events following those in the film. ''[[Bride of Frankenstein]]'' is an early example. When there are more films than one with the same characters, story arcs, or subject themes, these movies become a ''series'', such as the [[List of James Bond films|James Bond series]]. Existing outside a specific story timeline usually does not exclude a film from being part of a series. A film that portrays events occurring earlier in a timeline with those in another film, but is released after that film, is sometimes called a ''[[prequel]]'', an example being ''[[Butch and Sundance: The Early Days]]''.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

The ''credits'', or ''end credits'', are a list that gives credit to the people involved in the production of a film. Films from before the 1970s usually start a film with credits, often ending with only a title card, saying "The End" or some equivalent, often an equivalent that depends on the language of the production.{{Citation needed|date=January 2015}} From then onward, a film's credits usually appear at the end of most films. However, films with credits that end a film often repeat some credits at or near the start of a film and therefore appear twice, such as that film's acting leads, while less frequently some appearing near or at the beginning only appear there, not at the end, which often happens to the director's credit. The credits appearing at or near the beginning of a film are usually called ''titles'' or ''beginning titles''. A ''[[post-credits scene]]'' is a scene shown after the end of the credits. ''[[Ferris Bueller's Day Off]]'' has a post-credits scene in which Ferris tells the audience that the film is over and they should go home.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

A film's ''cast'' refers to a collection of the actors and actresses who appear, or ''star'', in a film. A ''star'' is an actor or actress, often a popular one, and in many cases, a [[celebrity]] who plays a central character in a film. Occasionally the word can also be used to refer to the fame of other members of the crew, such as a director or other personality, such as [[Martin Scorsese]]. A ''crew'' is usually interpreted as the people involved in a film's physical construction outside cast participation, and it could include directors, film editors, photographers, grips, gaffers, set decorators, prop masters, and costume designers. A person can both be part of a film's cast and crew, such as [[Woody Allen]], who directed and starred in ''[[Take the Money and Run (film)|Take the Money and Run]]''.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

A ''film goer'', ''movie goer'', or ''film buff'' is a person who likes or often attends films and movies, and any of these, though more often the latter, could also see oneself as a student to films and movies or the filmic process. Intense interest in films, film theory, and film criticism, is known as ''[[cinephilia]]''. A film enthusiast is known as a ''cinephile'' or ''cineaste''.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

=== Preview ===
{{Main|Test screening}}

''Preview performance'' refers to a showing of a film to a select audience, usually for the purposes of corporate promotions, before the public film premiere itself. Previews are sometimes used to judge audience reaction, which if unexpectedly negative, may result in recutting or even refilming certain sections based on the [[audience response]]. One example of a film that was changed after a negative response from the test screening is 1982's ''[[First Blood]]''. After the test audience responded very negatively to the death of protagonist [[John Rambo]], a [[Vietnam veteran]], at the end of the film, the company wrote and re-shot a new ending in which the character survives.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.yahoo.com/movies/bp/first-blood-turns-30-rambo-original-dark-end-174610790.html|title='First Blood' Turns 30: Rambo's original dark end|work=Yahoo |location=[[Yahoo! Movies]]|date=22 October 2012|access-date=16 November 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161117070040/https://www.yahoo.com/movies/bp/first-blood-turns-30-rambo-original-dark-end-174610790.html|archive-date=17 November 2016}}</ref>

=== Trailer and teaser ===
{{Main|Film trailer}}

''[[Trailer (promotion)|Trailers]]'' or ''previews'' are [[Advertising|advertisements]] for films that will be shown in 1 to 3 months at a cinema. Back in the early days of cinema, with theaters that had only one or two screens, only certain trailers were shown for the films that were going to be shown there. Later, when theaters added more screens or new theaters were built with a lot of screens, all different trailers were shown even if they were not going to play that film in that theater. Film studios realized that the more trailers that were shown (even if it was not going to be shown in that particular theater) the more patrons would go to a different theater to see the film when it came out. The term ''trailer'' comes from their having originally been shown at the end of a film program.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

That practice did not last long because patrons tended to leave the theater after the films ended, but the name has stuck. Trailers are now shown before the film (or the "A film" in a double feature program) begins. Film trailers are also common on [[DVD]]s and [[Blu-ray]] Discs, as well as on the Internet and mobile devices. Trailers are created to be engaging and interesting for viewers. As a result, in the Internet era, viewers often seek out trailers to watch them. Of the ten billion videos watched online annually in 2008, film trailers ranked third, after news and user-created videos.<ref>{{Cite web | url = https://awfj.org/2008/05/07/awfj-opinion-poll-all-about-movie-trailers/ | title = AWFJ Opinion Poll: All About Movie Trailers | publisher = AWFJ | date = 2008-05-09 | url-status=live | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131203011641/https://awfj.org/2008/05/07/awfj-opinion-poll-all-about-movie-trailers/ | archive-date = 2013-12-03 }}</ref> A ''teaser'' is a much shorter preview or advertisement that lasts only 10 to 30 seconds. Teasers are used to get patrons excited about a film coming out in the next six to twelve months. Teasers may be produced even before the film production is completed.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

== Culture ==
[[File:Mona_Zaki_2015.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Mona Zaki]], Egyptian film star, whose films influenced both the [[Culture of Egypt|Egyptian]] and [[Culture of Africa|African cultures]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-01-25 |title=Mona Zaki on Her Career's Future and Defending Women's Rights |url=https://en.vogue.me/culture/mona-zaki-vogue-arabia-interview/ |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=Vogue Arabia |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Actress Mona Zaki and key national authorities mark "The Egyptian Girl Celebration" with UNICEF during Gouna Film Festival |url=https://www.unicef.org/egypt/press-releases/actress-mona-zaki-and-key-national-authorities-mark-egyptian-girl-celebration-unicef |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=www.unicef.org |language=en}}</ref>]]

Films are [[cultural artifact]]s created by specific [[culture]]s, facilitating intercultural dialogue. It is considered to be an important art form that provides entertainment and historical value, often visually documenting a period of time. The visual basis of the medium gives it a universal power of communication, often stretched further through the use of [[Dubbing (filmmaking)|dubbing]] or [[subtitles]] to [[translation|translate]] the dialog into other languages.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Languages of Dubbing |chapter=How people greet each other in TV series and dubbing: Veronica Bonsignori, Silvia Bruti |date=2015 |doi=10.3726/978-3-0351-0809-5/13 |isbn=978-3-0343-1646-0 }}</ref> Just seeing a location in a film is linked to higher tourism to that location, demonstrating how powerful the suggestive nature of the medium can be.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tooke |first1=Nichola |last2=Baker |first2=Michael |title=Seeing is believing: the effect of film on visitor numbers to screened locations |journal=Tourism Management |date=March 1996 |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=87–94 |doi=10.1016/0261-5177(95)00111-5 }}</ref>

=== Education and propaganda ===
{{Main|Educational film|Propaganda film}}

Film is used for a range of goals, including education and propaganda due its ability to effectively intercultural dialogue. When the purpose is primarily educational, a film is called an "[[educational film]]". Examples are recordings of academic lectures and experiments, or a film based on a classic novel.

Film may be [[propaganda film|propaganda]], in whole or in part, such as the films made by [[Leni Riefenstahl]] in Nazi Germany, US war film trailers during World War II, or artistic films made under Stalin by [[Sergei Eisenstein]]. They may also be works of political protest, as in the films of [[Andrzej Wajda]], or more subtly, the films of [[Andrei Tarkovsky]]. The same film may be considered educational by some, and propaganda by others as the categorization of a film can be subjective.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

== Production ==
{{Main|Filmmaking}}

At its core, the means to produce a film depend on the content the filmmaker wishes to show, and the apparatus for displaying it: the [[zoetrope]] merely requires a series of images on a strip of paper. Film production can, therefore, take as little as one person with a camera (or even without a camera, as in [[Stan Brakhage]]'s 1963 film ''[[Mothlight]]''), or thousands of actors, extras, and crew members for a live-action, feature-length epic.
The necessary steps for almost any film can be boiled down to conception, planning, execution, revision, and distribution. The more involved the production, the more significant each of the steps becomes. In a typical [[production cycle]] of a Hollywood-style film, these main stages are defined as [[Script development|development]], [[pre-production]], [[Film production|production]], [[post-production]] and [[Film distributor|distribution]].{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

This production cycle usually takes three years. The first year is taken up with ''development''. The second year comprises ''preproduction'' and ''production''. The third year, ''post-production'' and ''distribution''. The bigger the production, the more resources it takes, and the more important [[Film budgeting|financing]] becomes; most [[feature film]]s are artistic works from the creators' perspective (e.g., [[film director]], [[cinematographer]], [[screenwriter]]) and for-profit business entities for the production companies.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

=== Crew ===
{{Main|Film crew}}

A film crew is a group of people hired by a film company, employed during the "production" or "photography" phase, for the purpose of producing a film or motion picture. ''Crew'' is distinguished from ''cast'', who are the [[actor]]s who appear in front of the [[camera]] or provide voices for characters in the film. The ''crew'' interacts with but is also distinct from the ''production staff'', consisting of producers, managers, company representatives, their assistants, and those whose primary responsibility falls in pre-production or post-production phases, such as [[screenwriter]]s and [[film editor]]s. Communication between ''production'' and ''crew'' generally passes through the director and his/her staff of assistants. Medium-to-large crews are generally divided into departments with well-defined hierarchies and standards for interaction and cooperation between the departments. Other than acting, the crew handles everything in the photography phase: props and costumes, shooting, sound, electrics (i.e., lights), sets, and production special effects. [[Caterer]]s (known in the film industry as "craft services") are usually not considered part of the crew.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

=== Technology ===
{{See also|Cinematic techniques}}

[[Film stock]] consists of transparent [[celluloid]], [[acetate]], or [[polyester]] [[film base|base]] coated with an emulsion containing light-sensitive chemicals. Cellulose nitrate was the first type of film base used to record motion pictures, but due to its flammability was eventually replaced by safer materials. Stock widths and the [[film format]] for images on the reel have had a rich history, though most large commercial films are still shot on (and distributed to theaters) as [[35mm movie film|35&nbsp;mm]] prints.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

Originally moving picture film was shot and projected at various speeds using hand-cranked [[movie camera|cameras]] and [[movie projector|projectors]]; though 1000 frames per minute ({{sfrac|16|2|3}} frame/s) is generally cited as a standard silent speed, research indicates most films were shot between 16 frame/s and 23 frame/s and projected from 18 frame/s on up (often reels included instructions on how fast each scene should be shown).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cinemaweb.com/silentfilm/bookshelf/18_car_1.htm |title=Silent Film Speed |publisher=Cinemaweb.com |date=1911-12-02 |access-date=2010-11-25 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070407224839/https://www.cinemaweb.com/silentfilm/bookshelf/18_car_1.htm |archive-date=April 7, 2007 }}</ref> When synchronized [[sound film]] was introduced in the late 1920s, a constant speed was required for the sound head. 24 frames per second were chosen because it was the slowest (and thus cheapest) speed which allowed for sufficient sound quality.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-12-29 |title=The Fi Hall of Fame: Hacking Film – Why 24 Frames Per Second? |url=https://www.filmindependent.org/blog/hacking-film-24-frames-per-second/ |access-date=2022-07-21 |website=Film Independent |language=en-US |archive-date=2022-07-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220721180326/https://www.filmindependent.org/blog/hacking-film-24-frames-per-second/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The standard was set with [[Warner Bros.]]'s [[The Jazz Singer]] and their [[Vitaphone]] system in 1927.<ref>[https://www.redsharknews.com/technology-computing/item/3881-why-24-frames-per-second-is-still-the-gold-standard-for-film Why 24 frames per second is still the gold standard for film]</ref><ref>[https://whatnerd.com/why-24-fps-standard-for-films/ Why Is 24 FPS the Standard for Films? Media Frame Rates, Explained]</ref> Improvements since the late 19th century include the mechanization of cameras&nbsp;– allowing them to record at a consistent speed, quiet camera design&nbsp;– allowing sound recorded on-set to be usable without requiring large "blimps" to encase the camera, the invention of more sophisticated [[film stock|filmstocks]] and [[Lens (optics)|lenses]], allowing [[Film director|directors]] to film in increasingly dim conditions, and the development of synchronized sound, allowing sound to be recorded at exactly the same speed as its corresponding action. The soundtrack can be recorded separately from shooting the film, but for live-action pictures, many parts of the soundtrack are usually recorded simultaneously.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

As a medium, film is not limited to motion pictures, since the technology developed as the basis for [[photography]]. It can be used to present a progressive sequence of still images in the form of a slideshow. Film has also been incorporated into [[multimedia]] presentations and often has importance as primary historical documentation. However, historic films have problems in terms of preservation and storage, and the motion picture industry is exploring many alternatives. Most films on cellulose nitrate base have been copied onto modern safety films. Some studios save color films through the use of [[separation masters]]: three B&W negatives each exposed through red, green, or blue filters (essentially a reverse of the [[Technicolor]] process). Digital methods have also been used to restore films, although their continued obsolescence cycle makes them (as of 2006) a poor choice for long-term preservation. [[Film preservation]] of decaying film stock is a matter of concern to both film historians and archivists and to companies interested in preserving their existing products in order to make them available to future generations (and thereby increase revenue). Preservation is generally a higher concern for nitrate and single-strip color films, due to their high decay rates; black-and-white films on safety bases and color films preserved on Technicolor imbibition prints tend to keep up much better, assuming proper handling and storage.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}

Some films in recent decades have been recorded using [[analog video]] technology similar to that used in [[television production]]. Modern [[digital video]] cameras and [[digital projector]]s are gaining ground as well. These approaches are preferred by some film-makers, especially because footage shot with [[digital cinema]] can be evaluated and edited with [[non-linear editing system]]s (NLE) without waiting for the film stock to be processed. The migration was gradual, and as of 2005, most major motion pictures were still shot on film.{{update after|2015|6|3}}

=== Independent ===
{{Main|Independent film}}

[[File:Fratelli Lumiere.jpg|thumb|left|upright|alt=Auguste and Louis Lumière brothers seated looking left|[[Auguste and Louis Lumière|The Lumière Brothers]], who were among the first filmmakers{{citation needed|date=August 2025}}]]

Independent filmmaking often takes place outside Hollywood, or other major [[studio system]]s. An independent film (or indie film) is a film initially produced without financing or distribution from a [[list of Hollywood movie studios|major film studio]]. Creative, business and technological reasons have all contributed to the growth of the indie film scene in the late 20th and early 21st century.
