ARTICLE: Filmmaking
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{Short description|Process of making a motion picture}}
{{use mdy dates|date=September 2026}}
{{Redirect|Filmmaker}}
{{More citations needed|date=April 2023}}
{{Filmmaking sidebar}}
[[File:Main Cast (206644687).jpeg|thumb|Film crew and cast members working together during principal photography]]
'''Filmmaking''', or '''film production''', is the process of creating a [[Film|motion picture]], for example, [[feature film]]s, episodic [[Serial (radio and television)|series]] for [[Streaming media|streaming]] and network [[broadcasting]], [[Television advertisement|commercials]] and advertisements, [[animation]]s, [[music video]]s, documentaries, or any other filmed product.<ref>Ascher, Steven, The Filmmaker’s Handbook, 5th Edition, Penguin Random House, 2019, pp. 1-2
</ref> It involves a number of distinct stages, including an initial story idea or commission, followed by [[screenwriting]], [[Casting (performing arts)|casting]], [[pre-production]], [[Principal photography|shooting]], [[Sound recording and reproduction|sound recording]], [[post-production]], and [[Film screening|screening]] the finished product before an audience, which may result in a [[film release]] distribution and exhibition. Generally, the process is nonlinear, in that the filmmaker typically shoots the script out of sequence, repeats shots as needed, and puts them together through editing later. Filmmaking takes place in a variety of economic, social, and political contexts around the world and uses a wide range of technologies and [[cinematic techniques]]. While originally films were recorded on [[photographic film]], most modern filmmaking is now [[digital cinematography|digital]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2013-01-09|title=The New World of Digital Filmmaking|url=https://www.filmconnection.com/reference-library/film-entrepreneurs/the-new-world-of-digital-filmmaking-0411/|access-date=2021-10-07|website=Film Connection Film Institute|language=en|archive-date=2021-10-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007204042/https://www.filmconnection.com/reference-library/film-entrepreneurs/the-new-world-of-digital-filmmaking-0411/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The production of a film typically consists of five major stages. The first is development, where the initial idea for the film is explored, rights to [[intellectual property]] (IP) may be secured, the [[screenplay]] is written, and financing is obtained. This is followed by [[pre-production]], where the arrangements and preparations for the shoot are made, including hiring cast and crew, scouting and securing locations, and constructing sets. The third stage is [[principal photography|production]], which is when the raw footage and other elements of the film are recorded.

After filming is complete, the project enters [[post-production]]. In this stage, the raw footage is edited, sound is mixed, [[visual effects]] are added, and a musical [[Film score|score]] is composed and recorded. The final stage is [[film distribution|distribution]], where the finished film is released to audiences. This involves marketing and promotion, and the film may be shown in [[Movie theater|cinemas]]/movie theaters, released on [[home video]], or made available through streaming services, cable, or television. Some filmmakers operate outside of the mainstream system and engage in [[independent filmmaking]], which has become more accessible with the advent of affordable digital technology and streaming platforms.

== Production stages ==
Film production consists of five major stages:<ref>{{cite book |last=Steiff |first=Josef |title=The Complete Idiot's Guide to Independent Filmmaking |publisher=Alpha Books |year=2005 |pages=26–28}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web | author = Roberts, Elaine  | orig-date = 2023-02-22 | date=2023-02-26 |title=The Stages of Film Production: From Script to Marketing |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/film-production-stages-76000/ |access-date=2026-06-18 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref>
* Development: Ideas for the film are created, rights to existing intellectual properties are purchased, and the screenplay is written. [[Finance|Financing]] for the project is sought and obtained.
* [[Pre-production]]: Arrangements and preparations are made for the shoot, such as hiring cast and [[film crew]], selecting locations, and constructing sets. 
* Production: The [[Footage|raw footage]] and other elements of the film are recorded during the film shoot, including [[principal photography]].
* [[Post-production]]: The images, sound, and visual effects of the recorded film are edited and combined into a finished product.
* [[Film distribution|Distribution]]: The completed film is distributed, marketed, and screened in cinemas and released on [[home video]] to be viewed at home.

=== Development ===
The development stage contains both general and specific components. Each [[film studio]] has a yearly retreat where their top [[creative executive]]s meet about a variety of areas and topics they wish to explore through collaborations with [[Film producer|producers]] and [[screenwriter]]s, and then ultimately, [[Film director|directors]], [[Actor|actors, and actresses]]. They choose trending topics from the media and real life, as well as other sources, to determine their yearly agenda. For example, in a year when [[Action film|action]] is popular, they may wish to explore that topic in one or more movies.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} Sometimes, they purchase the rights to articles, bestselling [[novel]]s, [[Play (theatre)|plays]], the [[Remake|remaking of older films]], stories with some basis in real life through a person or event, a [[video game]], [[fairy tale]], [[comic book]], or [[graphic novel]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |author=NYFA Staff |date=2023-10-06 |title=How is a Movie or Television Show Created and Produced? |url=https://www.nyfa.edu/student-resources/filming-movie-vs-filming-tv/ |access-date=2026-06-18 |website=[[New York Film Academy]] (NYFA) |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Likewise, research through surveys may inform their decisions. {{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} They may have had [[Blockbuster (entertainment)|blockbusters]] from their previous year and wish to explore a sequel. They will additionally acquire a completed and independently financed and produced film. 

Studios hold general meetings with producers and screenwriters about original story ideas. "It's become a lot more inclusive and expansive," a studio executive told [[TheWrap]]. “What used to happen was films were [[Greenlight|greenlit]] before the committee even met; it wasn't a collaborative process. Now you have three or four meetings. We beat it up quite a bit before we greenlight it." Studio executives can no longer green light one-third of their movies based on gut reaction to a project, [[Producers Guild of America|Producers Guild]] Co-chief [[Hawk Koch]] recalled: "There's not anybody who makes movies because their gut tells them to do it anymore," Koch said. "It's a focus group."<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Shaw |first=Brent Lang and Lucas |date=2013-11-20 |title=Who Has Greenlight Power in Hollywood? A Studio-by-Studio Guide |url=https://www.thewrap.com/hollywood-greenlighting-power/ |access-date=2026-06-18 |website=TheWrap |language=en-US}}</ref>

The executives return from the retreat with fairly well-established instructions. They spread these concepts through the industry community, especially to producers they have deals with (traditional studios will have those producers in offices on their lots). Also, agents for screenwriters are made aware. This results in a pairing of producers with [[writer]]s, where they develop a "take", a basic story idea that utilizes the concept given by studio executives. {{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} Often it is a competition with several pairings meeting with studio executives and "pitching" their "take." Very few writing jobs are from original ideas brought to studios by producers or writers.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} Completed original screenplays, referred to as "[[Spec script|specs]]," can make big news when they sell. However, these make up a small portion of movies that are ultimately produced, as projects based on existing IPs are seen as being "safer" by most studios.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Decline of Originality in Hollywood: a Look at the Numbers |url=https://www.parrotanalytics.com/press/the-decline-of-originality-in-hollywood-a-look-at-the-numbers/ |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=Parrot Analytics |language=en}}</ref>

Once the producer and writer have sold their approach to the desired subject matter, they begin to work. However, many writers and producers usually pass before a particular concept is realized in a way that is awarded a green light to production. Although it varies by project, on average, it takes several years to produce a film.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Holland |first=Stephen |date=2025-06-02 |title=Clint Eastwood Shelved Unforgiven for 10 Years - Because He Knew It Would Only Work Once He Was Old Enough |url=https://screenrant.com/clint-eastwood-unforgiven-movie-age-delay-factoid/ |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=ScreenRant |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Evangelista |first=Ron |date=2023-12-10 |title=Why Did It Take 20 Years for 'Unforgiven' To Get Made? |url=https://collider.com/unforgiven-clint-eastwood-production-history/ |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=Collider |language=en}}</ref> According to Xavier Luis Salinas, a line producer and unit production manager, “While in production, schedules can change at the turn of a dime, and you have to be ready to pivot right then and there. From the time you develop a script to a shooting script, you are looking at one to three years."<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2023-04-19 |title=How Long Does It Take to Film a Movie? |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/how-long-does-it-take-to-film-a-movie-76171/ |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref>

Writers have different styles and creative processes; some have stronger track records than others. Because of this, how the development process proceeds from there and how much detail a writer returns to the studio to divulge before beginning writing can vary greatly. Screenwriters are often protected by the union, the [[Writers Guild of America]] (WGA).<ref>{{Cite web |last=McNary |first=Dave |date=2017-04-03 |title=Writers Guild Takes Aim at Screenwriting Abuses in Contract Campaign |url=https://variety.com/2017/film/news/writers-guild-screenwriting-abuses-contract-campaign-1202021966/ |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=Variety |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Scherer |first=Matt |date=2023-10-17 |title=New WGA Labor Agreement Gives Hollywood Writers Important Protections in the Era of AI |url=https://cdt.org/insights/new-wga-labor-agreement-gives-hollywood-writers-important-protections-in-the-era-of-ai/ |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=Center for Democracy and Technology |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kinder |first=Molly |title=Hollywood writers went on strike to protect their livelihoods from generative AI. Their remarkable victory matters for all workers. |url=https://www.brookings.edu/articles/hollywood-writers-went-on-strike-to-protect-their-livelihoods-from-generative-ai-their-remarkable-victory-matters-for-all-workers/ |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=Brookings |language=en-US}}</ref> As of May 2025, the WGA allows a screenwriter to contract for a First Draft and a Revision.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Screen Compensation Guide |url=https://www.wga.org/members/employment-resources/writers-deal-hub/screen-compensation-guide |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=Writers Guild of America West |language=en}}</ref> In April 2026, the WGA was negotiating a deal with studios and streaming services to increase minimum payments for writers, improve the union's health plan, and more.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kilkenny |first=Katie |date=2026-04-08 |title=Writers Guild Reveals Details of Four-Year Deal: A $321M Health Plan Infusion, Higher Residuals and AI Licensing Language |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/writers-contract-deal-321m-health-plan-infusion-1236556126/ |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref> Preliminary discussions are minimal with studio executives but might be quite detailed with the producers.

Next, a [[screenwriter]] writes a [[screenplay]], typically over a period of several months; however, every writer's process and speed varies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Long Does it Take to Write a Screenplay? {{!}} No Film School |url=https://nofilmschool.com/how-long-does-it-take-to-write-a-screenplay |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=nofilmschool.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Deadlines are in their contracts, but historically there has been little pressure to adhere to them, given the "better late and great" rationale—though Warner Bros. attempted a crack down on screenwriters' late delivery dates in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jr |first=Mike Fleming |date=2010-06-18 |title=WHERE'S MY SCRIPT?! Warner Bros Cracks Down On Screenwriter's Late Delivery Dates |url=https://deadline.com/2010/06/wheres-my-script-warner-bros-cracks-down-on-writer-delivery-dates-47941/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=Deadline |language=en-US}}</ref> The screenwriter may rewrite the script several times to improve dramatization, clarity, structure, characters, dialogue, and overall style. 

A finished script undergoes [[script coverage]], where it is analyzed and graded before a report is written up (typically by interns or entry-level assistants or readers) to be given to higher-ups (producers, agents, and executives). Coverage is a way for young screenwriters to be read and may occur via agencies, studios, production companies, or a paid script coverage service or company.<ref>{{Cite web |last=nyfa|date=2017-12-29|title=Paid Script Coverage Services - The 2 Biggest Benefits and Drawbacks|url=https://www.nyfa.edu/student-resources/paid-script-coverage-services-the-2-biggest-benefits-and-drawbacks/|access-date=2026-06-22|website=NYFA|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Script Coverage: What It Is and How to Write It - EntertainmentCareers.Net Knowledge Base |url=https://help.entertainmentcareers.net/article/267-script-coverage-what-it-is-and-how-to-write-it |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=help.entertainmentcareers.net}}</ref>

The studio is the [[film distributor]] which, at an early stage, attempts to choose a slate of concepts that are likely to have market appeal and find potential financial success. [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]] distributors consider factors such as the [[film genre]], the target audience and assumed audience, the historical success of similar films, the actors who might appear in the film, and potential directors. All these factors imply a certain appeal of the film to a possible audience.<ref name=":1" /> Not all films make a profit from the theatrical release alone, however, the studio mainly targets the opening weekend and the second weekend to make most domestic profits. How long a film stays in cinemas depends largely on [[box office]] performance.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Stevenson |first=Rick |date=2025-09-23 |title=How Long Do Movies Stay In Theaters? It's Not Just About Ticket Sales |url=https://www.slashfilm.com/1954489/how-long-movies-stay-theaters/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=SlashFilm |language=en-US}}</ref> Occasionally, a film called a "word of mouth film" does not market strongly, but its success spreads by word of mouth. It slowly gains its audience.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McCormick |first=Colin |date=2022-08-15 |title=10 Indie Movies Whose Box Office Kept Growing By Word Of Mouth |url=https://screenrant.com/indie-movies-box-office-word-of-mouth/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=ScreenRant |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Yong |title=Word of Mouth for Movies: Its Dynamics and Impact on Box Office Revenue |journal=Journal of Marketing |date=2006 |volume=70 |issue=3 |pages=74–89 |doi=10.1509/jmkg.70.3.074}}</ref> These are special circumstances, but popular films may remain in theaters for months, while a typical run is closer to 30 to 45 days, which became the new norm following theater closures due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]—prior to which the standard theatrical run was 90 day.<ref name=":2" /> Further earnings result from [[pay television]] purchases, foreign market purchases and [[DVD]] sales to establish worldwide distribution gross of a film.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zipin |first=Dina |date=2025-11-03 |title=Understanding How Movies Generate Revenue Beyond Ticket Sales |url=https://www.investopedia.com/articles/investing/093015/how-exactly-do-movies-make-money.asp |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=Investopedia}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Fritz |first=Ben |date=2014-08-28 |title=For Hollywood, Not All Box Office Dollars Are Equal |url=http://online.wsj.com/articles/for-hollywood-not-all-box-office-dollars-are-equal-1409241925 |access-date=2026-06-22 |work=Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660}}</ref>

Once a screenplay is [[Greenlight|greenlit]], directors and actors are attached and the film proceeds into the pre-production stage, although sometimes development and pre-production stages will overlap. Projects that fail to obtain a green light may have protracted difficulties in making the transition to pre-production and enter a phase referred to as [[development hell]] for an extended period of time or until developmental [[turnaround (filmmaking)|turnaround]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Doyle |first=Barbara Freedman |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cPzhXug9X4oC&pg=PA55 |title=Make Your Movie: What You Need to Know About the Business and Politics of Filmmaking |date=2012-08-06 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1-136-07229-1 |language=en}}</ref> However, the average produced script can spend five to seven years in development.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Miyamoto |first=Ken |date=2017-05-16 |title=First Draft: Cover Your (Screenwriting) Ass With These Rules For Writing Valuable Script Coverage - MovieMaker Magazine |url=https://www.moviemaker.com/first-draft-script-coverage/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=www.moviemaker.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

Like almost any business venture, financing a film project deals with the management and procurement of financial resources to cover production costs. It includes the dynamics of the [[asset]]s required to fund the filmmaking and the [[Liability (financial accounting)|liabilities]] incurred during the filmmaking over the time period from early development through the management of profits and losses after distribution under conditions of different degrees of uncertainty and risk. The practical aspects of filmmaking finance can also be defined as the science of the money management of all phases involved in filmmaking. Film finance aims to price assets based on their risk level and their expected [[rate of return]] based upon anticipated profits and protection against losses.<ref>{{Cite web |title=IP assets and film finance – how it works in the United States |url=https://www.wipo.int/en/web/wipo-magazine/article-details/?assetRef=56463&title=ip-assets-and-film-finance-how-it-works-in-the-united-states |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=www.wipo.int |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Moore |first=Schuyler |title=Why Film Budgets Are Important, Beyond The Cost Of Production |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/schuylermoore/2019/04/13/the-importance-of-film-budgets/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-17 |title=How the US film industry mitigates financial risk |url=https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/how-us-film-industry-mitigates-financial-risk |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=CEPR |language=en}}</ref>

For major studios, the average cost to produce a movie is about $65 million.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Why Movies Cost So Much To Make |url=https://www.investopedia.com/financial-edge/0611/why-movies-cost-so-much-to-make.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260227061058/https://www.investopedia.com/financial-edge/0611/why-movies-cost-so-much-to-make.aspx |archive-date=2026-02-27 |access-date=2026-06-22 |work=Investopedia |language=en}}</ref> The total cost to make a film depends on several factors, including its genre. On average, the most expensive [[Film genre|movie genres]] are adventure, sci-fi, animation, and fantasy.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} Conversely, genres like music-based, horror, and romance typically have smaller average budgets.<ref>{{Cite web |last=CineVue |date=2020-11-18 |title=The true cost of movie-making |url=https://cine-vue.com/2020/11/the-true-cost-of-movie-making.html |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=CineVue |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Follows |first=Stephen |title=How much does the average movie cost to make? |url=https://stephenfollows.com/p/how-much-does-the-average-movie-cost-to-make |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=stephenfollows.com |date=8 July 2019 |language=en}}</ref> Also, finding funding generally takes longer for [[Independent film|independent films]], since they do not have that backing of a major studio.<ref name=":3" />

=== Pre-production ===
{{See also|Pre-production}}
Pre-production typically takes three to six months.<ref name=":0" /> In pre-production, every step of actually creating the film is carefully designed and planned. This is the phase for narrowing down all the options of the production. It is where all the planning takes place before the [[camera]] rolls and sets the overall vision of the project. Filmmaker [[Roger Corman]] said, "Take all the time you need in preproduction because you don’t want to be solving problems during shooting that you could’ve solved before shooting".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Macaulay |first=Scott |date=2015-08-10 |title=10 Lessons on Filmmaking from Roger Corman |url=https://filmmakermagazine.com/95125-10-lessons-on-filmmaking-from-roger-corman/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=Filmmaker Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> The [[production company]] will establish a [[production office]], which provides space for various crew members to work together.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Life in a Production Office: A Filmmaker's Survival Guide {{!}} No Film School |url=https://nofilmschool.com/survival-guide-production-office |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=nofilmschool.com |language=en-US}}</ref> The film is pre-visualized by the director and may be [[storyboard]]ed with the help of [[illustrator]]s and [[concept art]]ists.<ref>{{Cite web |last=PrintMag |date=2018-12-05 |title=Storyboarding: Drawing from Script to Screen |url=https://www.printmag.com/design-specialties/storyboarding-drawing-from-script-to-screen/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=PRINT Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Montoya |first=Karen |date=2023-11-21 |title=Using the Art of Storyboarding to Visualize Films |url=https://ibtcollege.com/virtualfilmschool/using-the-art-of-storyboarding-to-visualize-films/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=Virtual Film School |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Brine |first=Kelly Gordon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5Jv9DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA32 |title=The Art of Cinematic Storytelling: A Visual Guide to Planning Shots, Cuts, and Transitions |date=2020-09-18 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-005434-2 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> A [[production budget]] is drawn up to plan expenditures for the film.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Production Budget definition ,formula and Example {{!}} Accounting Details |url=http://www.accountingdetails.com/production_budget.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305103022/http://www.accountingdetails.com/production_budget.htm |archive-date=2016-03-05 |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=www.accountingdetails.com |language=en-US}}</ref> For major productions, [[insurance]] is procured to protect against accidents.<ref>{{Cite web |last=California |first=State of |date=2020-08-21 |title=Insurance Requirements |url=https://film.ca.gov/state-permits/insurance-requirements/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=California Film Commission |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Verdi |first=Thomas |date=2021-08-10 |title=Do I Really Need Film Insurance? |url=https://www.thefilmfund.co/do-i-really-need-film-insurance/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=The Film Fund |language=en-US}}</ref> Pre-production also includes working out the shoot location and casting process.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> The Producer hires a Line Manager or a Production Manager to create the schedule and budget for the film.<ref name=":0" />

The nature of the film, and the budget, determine the size and type of crew used during filmmaking. Many Hollywood [[Blockbuster (entertainment)|blockbusters]] employ a cast and [[Film crew|crew]] of hundreds or thousands,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Reid |first=Caroline |title=How Many People Does It Really Take To Make A Blockbuster Movie? |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/carolinereid/2024/11/08/how-many-people-does-it-really-take-to-make-a-blockbuster-movie/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref> while a low-budget, [[independent film]] may be made by a "skeleton crew" of eight or nine (or fewer).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kroll |first=Noam |date=2013-09-30 |title=The 5 People Filmmakers Need for a Tiny Skeleton Crew |url=https://www.indiewire.com/features/craft/the-5-people-filmmakers-need-for-a-tiny-skeleton-crew-34424/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=IndieWire |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-04-04 |title=The 10 People You Need on a Low-Budget Skeleton Crew |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/low-budget-production-crew-members-70478/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref> 

==== Crew positions ====
Common positions of a film crew include:<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-05-20 |title=Film Crew Positions: A Guide to Every Job on a Movie Set |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/film-crew-hierarchy-guide-75132/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref>
* [[Storyboard artist]]: The storyboard artist creates visual images to help the director and production designer communicate their ideas to the production team.<ref>{{Cite web |last=White |first=Anna |date=2014-03-03 |title=Britain's coolest jobs: the Hollywood storyboard artist |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/jobs/10672637/Britains-coolest-jobs-the-Hollywood-storyboard-artist.html |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=The Telegraph}}</ref> 
* [[Film director|Director]]: The director turns a script into a movie. They are primarily responsible for the overall storytelling, creative decisions, and acting of the film.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=The director - Roles and responsibilities - GCSE Moving Image Arts (CCEA) Revision |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/guides/zpd22p3/revision/2 |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=BBC Bitesize |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Director (also known as filmmaker) in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/development-film-and-tv-drama-job-profiles/director-film-and-tv-drama/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref>
** [[Assistant director]] (AD): The AD manages the [[shooting schedule]] and logistics of the production, among other tasks. There are several types of AD, each with different responsibilities.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last= |title=Assistant director in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/production-management/assistant-director/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0" />
* [[Film producer]]: The producer helps initiate and oversee the development of films by securing funding, working with the director, and hiring the cast and crew.<ref name=":5" />
** [[Unit production manager]] (UPM): The UPM manages the [[production budget]] and [[production schedule]]. They also report, on behalf of the production office, to the [[studio executives]] or financiers of the film.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-02-03 |title=How to Become a Unit Production Manager |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/unit-production-manager-70518/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref>
*** [[Location manager]]: The location manager finds and manages film locations.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Location manager job profile {{!}} Prospects.ac.uk |url=https://www.prospects.ac.uk/job-profiles/location-manager |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250811032523/https://www.prospects.ac.uk/job-profiles/location-manager |archive-date=2025-08-11 |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=www.prospects.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Locations manager in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/production-management/locations-manager/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref> Many movies feature segments that are shot in the controllable environment of a studio [[sound stage]], while outdoor sequences call for filming [[location shooting|on location]].
* [[Production designer]]: The production designer creates the visual conception of the film, working with the [[art director]], who manages the art department that makes production [[set (film and TV scenery)|sets]].<ref name="Vincent LoBrutto 1994" /><ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Production designer in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/craft/production-designer-film-and-tv-drama/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref>
** [[Costume designer]]: The costume designer creates the clothing for the characters in the film, working closely with the actors and other departments.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Costume designer in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/craft/costume-designer-film-and-tv-drama/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref>
** Makeup and hair designer: This designer works closely with the costume designer to create a specific look for a character.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Hair and make-up designer in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/craft/hair-and-make-up-designer-film-and-tv-drama/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref>
* [[Casting director]] (CD): The CD finds actors to fill the parts in the script. This normally requires actors to partake in an [[audition]], either live in front of the casting director or in front of one or more cameras.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Casting director in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/development-film-and-tv-drama-job-profiles/casting-director/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref>
** [[Choreographer]]: The choreographer creates and coordinates the film's movement and/or dance(s)—the latter typically being for musicals.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2005-01-01 |title=Choreographer {{!}} Berklee |url=https://www.berklee.edu/careers/roles/choreographer |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=www.berklee.edu |language=en}}</ref> Some films also credit a [[fight choreographer]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Maison |first=Jordan |date=2020-02-14 |title=Fight choreography: Planning and shooting your fight scenes |url=https://www.videomaker.com/how-to/planning/writing/fight-choreography-planning-and-shooting-your-fight-scenes/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Videomaker |language=en-US}}</ref>
* [[cinematographer|Director of photography (DOP)]]: The DOP is the head of the [[photography]] of the entire film, supervising all [[cinematographer]]s and [[camera operator]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Director of photography (DoP) in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/technical/director-of-photography-dop/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref>
* [[Production sound mixer]]: The production sound mixer is the head of the sound department during the production stage of filmmaking. They record and mix the audio on set—dialogue, [[Presence (sound recording)|presence]] and [[sound effects]] in [[monaural]] and [[Ambience (sound recording)|ambience]] in stereo.<ref>''Sound for Digital Video'' by Tomlinson Holman (Focal Press) 2005 (p. 162)</ref><ref>''Dialogue Editing for Motion Pictures'' by John Purcell (Focal Press) 2007 (p. 148)</ref> They work with the [[Boom operator (media)|boom operator]], Director, DA, DP, and First AD.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Sound mixer (also known as sound recordist) in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/technical/sound-mixer/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref>
** [[Sound designer]]: The sound designer creates the aural conception of the film,<ref name="Vincent LoBrutto 1994">Sound-On-Film by Vincent LoBrutto (1994)</ref> working with the [[Supervising Sound Editor|supervising sound editor]]. On [[Bollywood]]-style Indian productions, the sound designer plays the role of a [[director of audiography]] (DA).<ref>''Film Sound: Theory and Practice'', Edited by Elisabeth Weis and John Belton, Columbia University Press (1985). p. 361</ref>
** [[Composer]]: The composer reads the script, collaborates with director, and then creates new music for the film, called the [[Film score|score]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Music Industry Career Roles - Berklee Online |url=https://online.berklee.edu/careers-in-music/roles/composer-film |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=online.berklee.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Whittaker |first=Michael |date=2023-10-27 |title=The Process Of Creating A Film Score |url=https://filmscoreseminar.com/the-process-of-creating-a-film-score/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=Film Score Seminar |language=en-US}}</ref> The film's score may be composed before or after the movie finishes filming.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-04-05 |title=Which comes first, the movie or the music? |url=https://www.yourclassical.org/story/2014/11/05/film-score-picture |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=www.yourclassical.org |language=en}}</ref>

=== Production ===
{{see also|Cinematography|Audiography|Principal photography}}
[[File:Steven Spielberg with Chandran Rutnam in Sri Lanka.jpg|thumb|[[Steven Spielberg]] (standing) with [[Chandran Rutnam]] in Sri Lanka, during the production of ''[[Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom]]'' (released 1984)]]
[[File:Mahmoud_Zulfikar,_1968.jpg|alt=Mahmoud Zulfikar, 1968|thumb|[[Mahmoud Zulfikar]] during the production of ''[[The Splendor of Love]]'' (released 1968)]]
[[File:Filminspelning - Ystad-2022.jpg|thumb|A film production in [[Ystad]] 2022]]
Production can take five to eight weeks for a mid-range movie, or three to four weeks for a lower budget film.<ref name=":3" /> During production, the film's audio and video [[footage]] is captured. In this phase, it is key to keep planning ahead of the daily shoot. The primary aim is to stick to the budget and schedule, which requires constant vigilance.<ref name=":0" /> More crew will be recruited at this stage, such as the [[property master|property (prop) master]],<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Prop master in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/craft/prop-master/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref> [[script supervisor]],<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Script supervisor (also known as continuity) in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/technical/script-supervisor-film-and-tv-drama/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref> assistant directors,<ref name=":6" /> stills [[photographer]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-09-24 |title=What is a film stills, or unit stills photographer? - Film Stills Academy |url=https://filmstillsacademy.com/what-is-a-film-stills-or-unit-stills-photographer/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |language=en-NZ}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-08 |title=Unit Stills Photographer: The what and the How. |url=https://unitstillsdirectory.com/unit-stills-photographers-what-and-how/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |language=en-US}}</ref> [[film editor|picture editor]],<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Editor in the film and TV drama industries |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/post-production/editor-film-and-tv-drama/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref> and [[Sound editor (filmmaking)|sound editor]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Siebum |first=Doug |title=Tim Nielsen offers insight into the role of Supervising Sound Editor |url=https://www.asoundeffect.com/tim-nielsen-supervising-sound-editor/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=A Sound Effect}}</ref> These are the most common roles in filmmaking; the [[production office]] can create any unique blend of roles to suit the various responsibilities needed during the production of a film. Communication is key between the location, set, office, production company, distributors, and all other parties involved.<ref name=":0" />

A typical day shooting begins with the crew arriving on the set/location by their call time. [[Actor]]s usually have their own separate call times.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-30 |title=What Is a Call Time? Everything Actors Need to Know |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/call-time-meaning-75749/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref> Since set [[Set construction|construction]] can take weeks, depending on the size,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Torkildson |first=Adam |date=2023-05-18 |title=Movie Set Design and Construction: Bringing Imagination to Life |url=https://bombreport.com/movie-set-design-and-construction-bringing-imagination-to-life/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Bomb Report |language=en-US}}</ref> and set [[Set dresser|dressing]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-02-01 |title=How to Become a Set Dresser for Movies + TV |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/set-dresser-70516/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref> and [[lighting]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-06-06 |title=Film Lighting Techniques: A Guide for Directors + Cinematographers |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/film-lighting-techniques-76277/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref> can take many hours or even days, they are often done in advance.

The [[Grip (job)|grip]], electric and production design crews are typically a step ahead of the camera and sound departments.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DFI Rentals |url=https://www.dfirentals.com/news/the-grip-crew-explained |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=www.dfirentals.com}}</ref> For efficiency's sake, while a scene is being filmed, they are already preparing the next one.

While the crew prepares their equipment, the actors do their costumes and attend the hair and make-up departments. The actors rehearse the [[film script|script]] and [[Blocking (stage)|blocking]] with the director, and the camera and sound crews rehearse with them and make final tweaks.<ref>{{Cite web |last=nyfa |date=2023-12-12 |title=Mastering the 7 Stages of Film Production |url=https://www.nyfa.edu/student-resources/7-stages-film-production/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=NYFA |language=en-US}}</ref> Finally, the action is shot in as many [[take]]s as the director wishes. Most American productions follow a specific procedure:

The assistant director (AD) calls "picture is up!" to inform everyone that a take is about to be recorded, and then "quiet, everyone!" Once everyone is ready to shoot, the AD calls "roll sound" (if the take involves sound), and the [[production sound mixer]] will start their equipment, record a verbal slate of the take's information, and announce "sound speed", or just "speed", when they are ready. The AD follows with "roll camera", answered by "speed!" by the camera operator once the camera is recording. The [[clapper loader]], who is already in front of the camera with the [[clapperboard]], calls "marker!" and slaps it shut. If the take involves extras or background action, the AD will cue them ("action background!"), and last is the director, telling the actors "action!". The AD may echo "action" louder on large sets.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}}

A take is over when the director calls "Cut!" and the camera and sound stop recording.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cut |url=https://howtofilmschool.com/dictionary/cut-film-set/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=HowToFilmSchool.com |language=en-US}}</ref> The script supervisor will note any continuity issues, and the sound and camera teams log technical notes for the take on their respective report sheets. If the director decides additional takes are required, the whole process repeats.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tucker |first=Patrick |date=2013-02-03 |title=What A Film Director Does After They Say CUT |url=https://raindance.org/what-a-film-director-does-after-they-say-cut/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=Raindance |language=en-GB}}</ref> Once satisfied, the crew moves on to the next camera angle or "setup", until the whole scene is "covered." When shooting is finished for the scene, the assistant director declares a "wrap" or "moving on",<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=2014-01-30 |title=Film Studies 101: On-Set Jargon Explained |url=https://www.empireonline.com/movies/features/film-studies-101-film-terms-explained/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=Empire |language=en}}</ref> and the crew will "strike", or dismantle, the set for that scene.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Set Deconstruction - Strike {{!}} UCOP |url=https://www.ucop.edu/safety-and-loss-prevention/environmental/program-resources/performing-arts/strike.html |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=www.ucop.edu}}</ref>

At the end of the day, the director approves the next day's shooting schedule and a daily progress report is sent to the production office. This includes the report sheets from continuity, sound, and camera teams.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} [[Daily call sheet|Call sheet]]s are distributed to the cast and crew to tell them when and where to turn up the next shooting day.<ref name=":7" /> Later on, the director, producer, other department heads, and, sometimes, the cast, may gather to watch that day or yesterday's raw, unedited footage, called ''[[dailies]]'', and review their work.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Team |first=N. F. I. |date=2021-12-16 |title=Dailies - Everything You Need to Know |url=https://www.nfi.edu/dailies/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=NFI |language=en-US}}</ref>

With workdays often lasting for 12 to 18 hours,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Are Film and TV Set Hours Still Brutal? {{!}} No Film School |url=https://nofilmschool.com/film-and-tv-set-hours-brutal |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=nofilmschool.com |language=en-US}}</ref> film production tends to create a [[Team building|team spirit]]. When the entire film is "in the can", or in the completion of the production phase,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-06-17 |title=in the can |url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/us/dictionary/english/in-the-can |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=dictionary.cambridge.org |language=en-US}}</ref> it is customary for the production office to arrange a [[wrap party]], to thank all the cast and crew for their efforts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-07-01 |title=Scenes from the Game of Thrones series wrap party |url=https://winteriscoming.net/2018/07/01/scenes-from-the-game-of-thrones-series-wrap-party/ |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=Winter is Coming |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Watts |first=Halina |date=2019-09-28 |title='Really drunk' James Bond star Daniel Craig's emotional wrap party speech |url=https://www.mirror.co.uk/3am/celebrity-news/really-drunk-james-bond-star-20324808 |access-date=2026-06-23 |website=Daily Mirror |language=en}}</ref>

For the production phase on [[Live action|live-action films]], synchronizing work schedules of key cast and crew members is very important.<ref name="Wurmfeld_Page_52">{{cite book |last1=Wurmfeld |first1=Eden H. |last2=Laloggia |first2=Nicole |title=IFP/Los Angeles Independent Filmmaker's Manual |date=2004 |publisher=Elsevier |location=Amsterdam |isbn=9781136051067 |page=52 |edition=2nd |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OXMqBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA52 |access-date=28 June 2023 |archive-date=22 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230722162303/https://books.google.com/books?id=OXMqBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA52 |url-status=live }}</ref> For many scenes, several cast members and many crew members must be physically present at the same place at the same time (and [[bankable star]]s may need to rush from one project to another). Animated films have different workflow at the production phase, in that voice actors can record their takes in the [[recording studio]] at different times and may not see one another until the film's premiere.<ref name="Hayes_Page_176">{{cite book |last1=Hayes |first1=Derek |last2=Webster |first2=Chris |title=Acting and Performance for Animation |date=2013 |publisher=Focal Press |location=New York and London |isbn=9781136135989 |page=176 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4z0qBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA176 |access-date=2023-03-19 |archive-date=2023-04-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230409044929/https://books.google.com/books?id=4z0qBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA176 |url-status=live }}</ref> Animated films also have different crew, since most physical live-action tasks are either unnecessary or are simulated by various types of [[animator]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Draper |first=Jon |date=2020-02-16 |title=Live action vs Animation: A Comparison • Stormy Studio |url=https://stormystudio.com/live-action-vs-animation-a-comparison/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Stormy Studio |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Animator in the animation industry |url=https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/animation/production/animator-animation/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=ScreenSkills |language=en}}</ref>

=== Post-production ===
{{main|Post-production}}

Post-production can take days to years, depending on the specific film, as well as the time and resources available. This stage is usually thought of as starting when principal photography ends, but they may overlap. The bulk of post-production consists of the [[film editor]] reviewing the footage with the director and assembling the film out of selected takes. The production sound (dialogue) is also edited; music tracks and songs are composed and recorded if a film is intended to have a [[Film score|score]]; sound effects are designed and recorded. Any computer-generated visual effects are digitally added by an [[artist]].<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |date=2022-08-09 |title=Postproduction 101: Everything That Happens After Filming Wraps |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/postproduction-overview-crew-guide-74445/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref> Finally, all sound elements are mixed down into "stems", which are synchronized to the images on the screen.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-12 |title=What are Stems in Music Production? |url=https://www.ism.org/advice/what-are-stems-in-music-production/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Independent Society of Musicians |language=en-GB}}</ref> There will be a [[rough cut]], a fine cut, and then a "[[picture lock]]", where the editor and director agree on the film’s final cut, which is when it is ready to be distributed and shown to audiences.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nicole |date=2025-08-05 |title=Why is Picture Lock Important in Film Editing? |url=https://beverlyboy.com/filmmaking/why-is-picture-lock-important-in-film-editing/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=BeverlyBoy Productions |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2023-03-09 |title=From Assembly to Picture Lock - Rough Cut, Fine Cut, and Final Cut |url=https://www.filmsupply.com/articles/rough-fine-final-cut/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Filmsupply Blog |language=en-US}}</ref>

Post-production may be completed by a studio's, media company's, or agency's in-house postproduction team, individual freelancers hired for specific roles, or an outsourced postproduction company. Common digital tools used for post-production may include [[Adobe Premiere Pro|Adobe Premiere]], [[Media Composer|Avid's Media Composer]], [[Final Cut Pro]], [[Adobe After Effects]], and [[Lightworks]].<ref name=":8" />

===Distribution===
{{main|Film distribution}}

Distribution is the last stage, where the film is released in [[movie theater]]s, for direct download or [[Streaming media|streaming]] from a [[digital media]] provider, [[direct-to-video]] physical media (like [[VHS]], [[VCD]], [[DVD-Video|DVD]], [[Blu-ray]]), or a hybrid of these.<ref name=":0" /> The film is duplicated as required (either onto film or [[hard disk drive]]s) and distributed in cinemas for exhibition (screening). 

Marketing is also an essential element of this phase. [[Press kit|Press kits]], [[Film poster|posters]], and other advertising materials are published, and the film is advertised and [[Film promotion|promoted]] via [[Trailer (promotion)|trailers]], social media campaigns, and TV spots.<ref name=":0" /> A [[B-roll]] clip may be released to the press based on raw footage shot for a [[Behind-the-scenes|"making of" documentary]], which may include making-of clips as well as on-set interviews separate from those of the production company or distributor.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sciretta |first=Peter |date=2010-11-03 |title=VOTD: Watch David Fincher Direct 'The Social Network' |url=https://www.slashfilm.com/512006/watch-david-fincher-direct-the-social-network/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=SlashFilm |language=en-US}}</ref> For major films, key personnel are often contractually required to participate in promotional tours in which they appear at premieres and festivals and sit for interviews with many TV, print, and online journalists.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Controlling the Spotlight: Promotional Clauses in Performance Contracts |url=https://www.agg.com/news-insights/publications/controlling-the-spotlight-promotional-clauses-in-performance-contracts/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Arnall Golden Gregory LLP |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Rubin |first=Rebecca |date=2025-12-11 |title=Can Timothée Chalamet Save Indie Film? Inside 'Marty Supreme's' Wild Press Tour |url=https://variety.com/2025/film/news/timothee-chalamet-marty-supreme-press-tour-1236605298/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Variety |language=en-US}}</ref> In some cases, a prop from the film may be used to help promote a film—for example, the 40-foot [[Trojan Horse|Trojan horse]] from ''[[The Odyssey (2026 film)|The Odyssey]]'' (2026).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trojan Horse Pops Up in Arlington to Promote New Movie 'The Odyssey' |url=https://www.arlingtontx.gov/News-Articles/2026/June/Trojan-Horse-Pops-Up-in-Arlington-to-Promote-New-Movie-The-Odyssey |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=www.arlingtontx.gov |language=en-US}}</ref> Large productions may require more than one promotional tour to rejuvenate audience demand at each release window.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Zuckerman |first=Esther |date=2025-11-21 |title='Wicked' and the Never-Ending Press Tour |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/21/movies/wicked-for-good-2-ariana-grande-cynthia-erivo.html |access-date=2026-06-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

Since the advent of [[home video]] in the late 1970s, most major films have followed a pattern of having several distinct release windows. A film may first be released to [[Limited theatrical release|a few select cinemas]], or if it [[test screening|tests well enough]], may go directly into [[wide release]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hood |first=Cooper |date=2026-01-06 |title=Theaters Vs. Streaming: Breaking Down How Major Studios Handled Theatrical Windows & Release Gaps In 2025 |url=https://screenrant.com/movie-studios-2025-theatrical-release-windows-explainer/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=ScreenRant |language=en}}</ref> Next, it is released, normally at different times several weeks (or months) apart, into different market segments like [[video rental shop|rental]], [[retail]], [[pay-per-view]], [[in-flight entertainment]], [[cable television]], [[satellite television]], or [[free-to-air]] broadcast television. The distribution rights for the film are also usually sold for worldwide distribution. The distributor and the production company share profits and manage losses.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Moore |first=Schuyler |title=The 9 Types Of Film Distribution Agreements |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/schuylermoore/2019/07/19/types-of-film-distribution-agreements/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-06-08 |title=Film Distribution, Distribution Rights & Revenues Management |url=https://zannonimedia.com/film-distribution-rights-revenues/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Zannoni Media Advisors |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-13 |title=Film Rights Explained for Filmmakers {{!}} Domestic, International & Worldwide Deals |url=https://www.filmmakingstuff.com/film-rights-explained-what-filmmakers-need-to-know-before-signing-a-deal/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Film Making Stuff |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Independent filmmaking ==
{{main|Independent film}}

[[File:Sound recordist Curtis Choy.jpg|thumb|Sound recordist Curtis Choy (left) on location for ''[[Dim Sum: A Little Bit of Heart]]'', an indie film by director Wayne Wang (center) on Clement Street in the Richmond District of San Francisco, California 1983]]
 
Filmmaking also takes place outside of the mainstream, and this is commonly called [[independent filmmaking|independent ("indie") filmmaking]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-07-09 |title=How to Make an Indie Film |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/how-to-indie-film-786/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=www.backstage.com |language=en}}</ref> Since the introduction of [[DV (video format)|digital video]] (DV) technology, the means of production have become more democratized and economically viable.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DV – A SUCCESS STORY |url=http://www.stanford.edu/~hbreit/CILECT/DV_Report.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041027052504/http://www.stanford.edu/~hbreit/CILECT/DV_Report.htm |archive-date=2004-10-27 |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=www.stanford.edu}}</ref> Filmmakers can conceivably shoot and edit a film, create and edit the sound and music, and mix the final cut on a home computer. However, while the means of production may be democratized, financing, traditional distribution, and marketing remain difficult to accomplish outside the traditional system.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":9" /> 

In the past, most independent filmmakers relied on [[film festival]]s (such as [[Sundance Film Festival]], [[Venice Film Festival]], [[Cannes Film Festival]], and [[Toronto International Film Festival]]s) to get their films noticed and sold for distribution and production.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=The New Reality for Independent Filmmakers: Navigating a Transformed Industry Landscape in 2025 |url=https://www.marklitwak.com/the-new-reality-for-independent-filmmakers-navigating-a-transformed-industry-landscape-in-20251.html |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=Entertainment Law Resources |language=en}}</ref> However, the [[internet]] has allowed for the relatively inexpensive distribution of independent films on websites such as [[YouTube]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Forbes |first=Mercedes Diane Griffin |date=2023-04-26 |title=10 Short Independent Films on YouTube That Will Blow Your Mind |url=https://dgspeaks.com/10-short-independent-films-on-youtube-that-will-blow-your-mind/,%20https://dgspeaks.com/10-short-independent-films-on-youtube-that-will-blow-your-mind/ |access-date=2026-06-24 |website=DG Speaks |language=en-US}}</ref> As a result, several companies have emerged to assist filmmakers in getting independent movies seen and sold via mainstream internet marketplaces, often adjacent to popular Hollywood titles. With internet movie distribution, independent filmmakers who choose to forego a traditional distribution deal now have the ability to reach global audiences.<ref name=":9" />

======================================================================
ARTICLE: History of film
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{About|the history of film as an artistic medium|the history of motion-picture technology|History of film technology}}
{{Multiple issues|
{{very long|date=January 2026|words=15,117}}
{{More citations needed|date=September 2025}}
}}
{{Filmmaking sidebar|Related}}
The '''history of film''' chronicles the artistic and cultural development of a [[visual art|visual art form]] that uses [[history of film technology|film technologies]] that began in the late 19th century, influenced by the existing screen culture of magic lantern shows, and by traditions in photography, theater, and other popular media.

The advent of film as an artistic medium is not clearly defined. There were moving picture screenings long before the commercial, public screening of ten [[Auguste and Louis Lumière|Lumière brothers]]' short films in Paris on 28 December 1895, which has generally been regarded as the breakthrough of projected [[cinematography|cinematographic]] motion pictures. The earliest films were typically in [[black and white]], under a minute long, without recorded sound, and consisted of a single shot from a steady camera. The first decades saw film move from a novelty, to an established mass entertainment industry, with [[film production companies]] and studios established throughout the world. Conventions toward a general cinematic language developed, with film editing, camera movements and other [[cinematic techniques]] contributing specific roles in the [[narrativity|narrative]] of films.

Popular new media, including television (mainstream since the 1950s), [[home video]] (1980s), and the internet (1990s), influenced the distribution and consumption of films. Film production usually responded with content to fit the new media, technical innovations (including [[widescreen]] (1950s), 3D, and [[4D film]]), and more spectacular films to keep theatrical screenings attractive. Systems that were cheaper and more easily handled (including [[8mm film]], video, and [[smartphone camera]]s) allowed for an increasing number of people to create films of varying qualities, for any purpose including [[home movies]] and [[video art]], outside the conventions of the production systems of big studios. The technical quality tended to be lower than professional movies, but improved with [[digital video]] and affordable, high-quality [[digital camera]]s. Improving over time, digital production methods became more popular during the 1990s, resulting in increasingly realistic [[visual effects]] and popular feature-length [[computer animation]]s.

Various [[film genre]]s have emerged during the history of film, and enjoyed variable degrees of success.

== Precursors ==
{{Main|Precursors of film}}

The use of film as an art form traces its origins to several earlier traditions in the arts such as (oral) [[storytelling]], literature, theatre, opera, and visual arts. [[Cantastoria]] and similar ancient traditions combined storytelling with series of images that were shown or indicated one after the other. Predecessors to film that had already used light and shadows to create art before the advent of modern film technology include [[Shadowgraphy (performing art)|shadowgraphy]], [[Shadow play|shadow puppetry]], [[camera obscura]], and the [[magic lantern]].

Around 1790, old traditions of charlatans and entertainers using camera obscura or magic lantern to project images of demons or ghosts were further developed into a type of multimedia show known as [[phantasmagoria]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Ruffles |first=Tom |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BIL2BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA15 |title=Ghost Images: Cinema of the Afterlife |date=27 September 2004 |isbn=9780786420056 |pages=15–17|publisher=McFarland }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Meier |first=Allison C. |date=12 May 2018 |title=The Magic Lantern Shows that Influenced Modern Horror |url=https://daily.jstor.org/the-magic-lantern-shows-that-influenced-modern-horror/ |access-date=15 August 2020 |website=JSTOR Daily |language=en-US}}</ref> These popular shows entertained audiences using mechanical slides, rear projection, mobile projectors, [[superimposition]], [[Dissolve (filmmaking)|dissolves]], live actors, smoke (on which projections may have been cast), odors, sounds and even electric shocks.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Castle |first=Terry |date=1988 |title=Phantasmagoria: Spectral Technology and the Metaphorics of Modern Reverie |journal=Critical Inquiry |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=26–61 |doi=10.1086/448473 |issn=0093-1896 |jstor=1343603 |s2cid=162264583}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mannoni |first1=Laurent |last2=Brewster |first2=Ben |date=1996 |title=The Phantasmagoria |journal=Film History |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=390–415 |issn=0892-2160 |jstor=3815390}}</ref> While the earliest magic lantern shows were often designed to frighten viewers, advances by projectionists allowed for creative and even educational storytelling that could appeal to wider family audiences.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eisenhauer |first=Jennifer F. |date=2006 |title=Next Slide Please: The Magical, Scientific, and Corporate Discourses of Visual Projection Technologies |journal=Studies in Art Education |volume=47 |issue=3 |pages=198–214 |doi=10.2307/25475781 |issn=0039-3541 |jstor=25475781|doi-access=free }}</ref> New magic lantern techniques such as the use of [[dissolving views]] allowed for smoother transitions between two projected images and aided in providing stronger narratives, while [[chromatrope]]s provided colourful animations of intricate abstract patterns.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Marsh |first=Joss |title=Cinematicity in Media History |publisher=Edinburgh University Press |year=2013 |isbn=9780748676118 |editor-last=Geiger |editor-first=Jeffrey |page=23 |chapter=Dickensian 'Dissolving Views': The Magic Lantern, Visual Story-telling and the Victorian Technological Imagination |jstor=10.3366/j.ctt9qdrrf.7 |editor-last2=Littau |editor-first2=Karin |chapter-url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.3366/j.ctt9qdrrf.7}}</ref>

In 1833, scientific study of a [[Stroboscopic effect|stroboscopic]] illusion in spoked wheels by [[Joseph Plateau]], [[Michael Faraday]] and [[Simon Stampfer]] led to the invention of the Fantascope, also known as the stroboscopic disk or the [[phenakistiscope]], which was popular in several European countries for a while. Plateau thought it could be further developed for use in phantasmagoria and Stampfer imagined a system for longer scenes with strips on rollers, as well as a transparent version (presumably associated with projection). Plateau, [[Charles Wheatstone]], [[Antoine Claudet]] and others tried to combine the technique with the [[stereoscope]] (introduced in 1838) and photography (introduced in 1839) for a more complete illusion of reality, but until innovations in photo-sensitive chemicals and technologies to exchange the pictures allowed sharp recordings of sequences, such experiments relied on [[stop motion]] techniques to depict simple periodic movements.

{{multiple image
| align             = right
| width1            = 253
| image1            = The Horse in Motion.jpg
| caption1          = Eadweard Muybridge's ''The Horse in Motion'' cabinet cards utilized the technique of [[chronophotography]] to study motion.
| width2            = 155
| image2            = Electrotachyscope1.jpg
| caption2          = An Anschütz [[electrotachyscope]]
}}

With the 1878 publication of ''[[The Horse in Motion]]'' cabinet cards, [[Eadweard Muybridge]] introduced a method to record motion sequences that became known as [[chronophotography]]. Muybridge and later chronophotographers, like [[Étienne-Jules Marey]], [[Georges Demenÿ]], [[Albert Londe]], and [[Ottomar Anschütz]], almost exclusively used the technique for scientific study of locomotion of animals and humans. In 1880, Muybridge started lecturing on animal locomotion and used his [[Zoopraxiscope]] to project animations of the contours of his recordings, traced onto glass discs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lawrence |first=Amy |date=2003 |title=Counterfeit Motion: The Animated Films of Eadweard Muybridge |journal=Film Quarterly |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=15–25 |issn=0015-1386 |jstor=10.1525/fq.2004.57.2.15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Latsis |date=2015 |title=Landscape in Motion: Muybridge and the Origins of Chronophotography |journal=Film History |volume=27 |issue=3 |page=2 |doi=10.2979/filmhistory.27.3.1 |jstor=10.2979/filmhistory.27.3.1 |s2cid=194973091}}</ref> In 1887, Anschütz started presenting his chronophotographic recordings in motion with his [[Electrotachyscope]], displaying short loops on a small milk glass screen. By 1891, he had started mass production of a more economical, coin-operated peep-box viewing device of the same name that was exhibited at international exhibitions and fairs, including the 1893 [[World's Columbian Exposition|Chicago World's Fair]], or for longer periods at for instance the Berlin Exhibition Park (with nearly 34,000 paying visitors in summer 1892), at [[The Crystal Palace]] in London, and in several U.S. stores. Shifting the focus of the medium from technical and scientific interest in motion to entertainment for the masses, he recorded wrestlers, dancers, acrobats, scenes of everyday life, and probably some staged comical sequences. Extant records suggest some of his output directly influenced later works by the Edison Company, such as the 1894 film ''[[Fred Ott's Sneeze]]''.<ref name="copycats">{{Cite journal |last=Rossell |first=Deac |title=Copycats: Anschütz Chronophotographs as Direct Source Materials for Early Edison Kinetoscope Films |journal=Film History |year=2016 |volume=28 |issue=2 |page=142 |doi=10.2979/filmhistory.28.2.06 |s2cid=192159745 |url=https://www.academia.edu/28339416 |language=en}}</ref>

From October 1892 to March 1900, inventor [[Charles-Émile Reynaud|Émile Reynaud]] exhibited his [[Théâtre Optique]] ("Optical Theatre") film system at the [[Musée Grévin]] in Paris. Reynaud's screenings of animated stories such as ''[[Pauvre Pierrot]]'' and ''[[Autour d'une cabine]]'' were accompanied by live music, songs and some synchronised sound effects, and attracted over 500,000 visitors over the course of 12,800 shows.<ref name="emilereynaud.fr">{{cite web |date=11 November 2008 |title=Le Théâtre optique – Émile Reynaud |url=http://www.emilereynaud.fr/index.php/post/Le-Theatre-optique |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081111172705/http://www.emilereynaud.fr/index.php/post/Le-Theatre-optique |archive-date=11 November 2008}}</ref><ref name="myrent1989">{{Cite journal |last1=Myrent |first1=Glenn |year=1989 |title=Emile Reynaud: First Motion Picture Cartoonist |journal=Film History |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=191–202 |jstor=3814977}}</ref>

[[Thomas Edison|Edison's]] [[Kinetoscope]] peep-box viewer, mostly developed by lab assistant [[William Kennedy Dickson]], was introduced to the public in 1893,<ref name=":0" /> with images on celluloid loops showing about half a minute of motion picture entertainment,<ref name="Cook-1990" /> mostly performed by well-known vaudeville acts in the company's [[Edison's Black Maria|Black Maria studio]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Grainge |first1=Paul |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.3366/j.ctt1r28dt |title=Film Histories: An Introduction and Reader |last2=Jancovich |first2=Mark |last3=Monteith |first3=Sharon |date=2007 |publisher=Edinburgh University Press |isbn=978-0-7486-1906-1 |jstor=10.3366/j.ctt1r28dt }}</ref> The Kinetoscope quickly became a global sensation with multiple viewing parlors across major cities by 1895.<ref name=":0" /> As the initial novelty of the images wore off, the Edison Company was slow to diversify their repertoire of films and waning public interest caused business to slow by Spring 1895. To remedy declining profits, experiments, such as ''[[The Dickson Experimental Sound Film]]'', were conducted in an attempt to achieve Edison's original goal of combining the [[phonograph]] with visual recordings. Limitations in syncing the sound to the visuals, however, prevented widespread application.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Musser |first=Charles |title=Before the nickelodeon: Edwin S. Porter and the Edison Manufacturing Company |date=1991 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-06080-7 |series=The UCLA Film and Television Archive studies in history, criticism, and theory |location=Berkeley |pages=53–56}}</ref> During that same period, inventors began advancing technologies towards [[Movie projector|film projection]] that would eventually overtake Edison's peep-box format.<ref name=":1" />

On 25, 29 and 30 November 1894, Anschütz projected moving images from [[Electrotachyscope]] discs on a large screen in the darkened Grand Auditorium of a Post Office Building in Berlin.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.ottomar-anschuetz.de/kino_1__vorfuehrung.htm | title=Ottomar Anschütz, Kinogeschichte, lebender Bilder, Kino, erste-Kinovorführung, Kinovorführung, Projektion, Kinoe, Bewegungsbilder }}</ref> From 22 February to 30 March 1895, a commercial 1.5-hour program of 40 different scenes was screened for audiences of 300 people at the old Reichstag and received circa 4,000 visitors.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ottomar Anschütz, Kinogeschichte, lebender Bilder, Kino, erste-Kinovorführung, Kinovorführung, Projektion, Kinoe, Bewegungsbilder |url=http://www.ottomar-anschuetz.de/kino_1__vorfuehrung.htm |access-date=19 April 2020 |website=www.ottomar-anschuetz.de}}</ref>

== Novelty era (1890s – early 1900s) ==

=== Early projection, proliferation of actualities and newsreels ===
{{Main|Actuality film}}
[[File:Roundhay Garden Scene (1888) 7fps.webm|thumb|right|''[[Roundhay Garden Scene]]'' (1888) by [[Louis Le Prince]]]]
[[File:La Sortie de l'Usine Lumière à Lyon I 1895.webm|thumb|La Sortie de l'Usine Lumière à Lyon]]
Throughout the late 19th century, several inventors such as [[Wordsworth Donisthorpe]], [[Louis Le Prince]], [[William Friese-Greene]], and the [[Max Skladanowsky|Skladanowsky brothers]] developed devices that could capture and project moving images. The scenes in these experiments primarily served to demonstrate the technology itself and were usually filmed with family, friends or passing traffic as subjects.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fischer |first=Paul |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/on1201301040 |title=The man who invented motion pictures: a true tale of obsession, murder, and the movies |date=2022 |publisher=Simon & Schuster |isbn=978-1-9821-1482-4 |edition=1st |location=New York |oclc=on1201301040}}</ref> Initial advertisements promoted the devices used to screen films rather than the films themselves. As the technologies became more familiar to audiences, their potential for capturing and recreating events was exploited primarily in the form of actualities and [[newsreel]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=de Klerk |first=Nico |date=1999 |title=A Few Remaining Hours: News Films and the Interest in Technology in Amsterdam Film Shows, 1896–1910 |journal=Film History |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=5–17 |issn=0892-2160 |jstor=3815253}}</ref> Actualities began as a "series of views" that often contained shots of beautiful and lively places or performance acts. During the creation of these films, cinematographers often drew upon previously established [[Aesthetics|aesthetic]] values, such as [[Framing (visual arts)|framing]].  Due to the short length (often only one shot) of many actualities, catalogue records indicate that production companies marketed to exhibitors by promoting multiple actualities with related subject matters that could complement each other.<ref name="Turvey-2004">{{Cite journal |last=Turvey |first=Gerry |date=2004 |title=Panoramas, Parades and the Picturesque: The Aesthetics of British Actuality Films, 1895–1901 |journal=Film History |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=9–27 |doi=10.2979/FIL.2004.16.1.9 |issn=0892-2160 |jstor=3815556}}</ref> To enhance the viewers' experience, showings could be accompanied by live musicians in an orchestra, a theatre organ, live [[sound effect]]s and commentary spoken by the showman or projectionist.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Rothstein |first1=Edward |last2=B |first2=S.-Ilent Films Were Never Silent When the Evil Landlord Twirled His Moustache |date=8 February 1981 |title= Silent Films Had a Musical Voice |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/08/movies/silent-films-had-a-musical-voice.html |access-date=4 November 2021 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=American Cinema 1890–1909: Themes and Variations |date=2009 |publisher=Rutgers University Press |isbn=978-0-8135-4442-7 |jstor=j.ctt5hhz03}}</ref> Films were mostly screened inside temporary storefront spaces, in tents of traveling exhibitors at fairs, or as "dumb" acts in vaudeville programs.<ref>{{cite web |title=Birth of An Industry: Blackface Minstrelsy and the Rise of American Animation: Vaudeville and the Movies |publisher = USC.edu|url=https://scalar.usc.edu/works/birthofanindustry/vaudeville-in-the-movies|first = Nicholas |last =Sammond | work=Birth of An Industry: Blackface Minstrelsy and the Rise of American Animation }}</ref>

The early era of filmmaking, dubbed "the cinema of attractions" by film historian Tom Gunning, offered a relatively cheap and simple way of providing entertainment to the masses, with relatively little attention to story-telling.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gunning |first=Tom |chapter=The Cinema of Attraction[s]: Early Film, Its Spectator and the Avant-Garde |date=2006 |title=The Cinema of Attractions Reloaded |publisher=Amsterdam University Press |isbn=978-90-5356-945-0 |editor-last=Strauven |editor-first=Wanda |pages=381–388 |jstor=j.ctt46n09s.27}}</ref> Film was rarely recognized as an art form by exhibitors or audiences. Regarded by the upper class as a "vulgar" and "lowbrow" form of cheap entertainment, films largely appealed to the working class and were often too short to hold any strong narrative potential.<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Routledge companion to film history |date=2011 |editor=William Howard Guynn |isbn=978-1-136-89939-3 |location= New York |oclc=1241889104}}</ref> 

[[File:L'ArroseurArrosé.jpg|thumb|A frame from the Lumière brothers staged comedy film, ''[[L'Arroseur Arrosé]]'' (1895)]]

The first paying audience for a motion picture gathered at Madison Square Garden to see a staged actuality that purported itself to be a boxing fight filmed by [[Woodville Latham]] using a device called the [[Eidoloscope]] on May 20, 1895. Commissioned by Latham, the French inventor [[Eugene Augustin Lauste]] created the device with additional expertise from [[William Kennedy Dickson]] and crafted a mechanism that came to be known as the [[Latham loop]], which allowed for longer continuous runtimes and was less abrasive on the celluloid film.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Encyclopedia of Early Cinema |date=2004-03-01 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-56676-1 |editor-last=Abel |editor-first=Richard |doi=10.4324/9780203482049}}</ref>

The first public screening by [[Lumière brothers|Auguste and Louis Lumière]], on December 28, 1895, consisted of ten films and lasted roughly 20 minutes. It mainly presented actualities, such as ''[[Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory]]'', but the show also included the staged comedy ''[[L'Arroseur Arrosé]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Film History Before 1920 |url=https://www.filmsite.org/pre20sintro2.html |access-date=20 October 2021 |website=www.filmsite.org}}</ref> The [[Cinematograph|Cinématographe]] was an instant success, bringing in an average of 2,500 to 3,000 francs daily by the end of January 1896.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Rossell |first=Deac |date=1995 |title=A Chronology of Cinema, 1889–1896 |journal=Film History |volume=7 |issue=2 |page=140 |issn=0892-2160 |jstor=3815166}}</ref> Following the first screening, the order and selection of films were changed often.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Sklar |first=Robert |title=A world history of film |date=2002 |publisher=Harry N. Abrams |isbn=0-8109-0606-6 |edition=2nd |location=New York |page=26 |oclc=46713129}}</ref> Following the success of their 1895 screening, The Lumière brothers sent cameramen across the world to capture new subjects for presentation. After the cinematographer shot scenes, they often exhibited their recordings locally and then sent them back to the company factory in Lyon to make duplicate prints for sale to whoever wanted them.<ref>{{cite book |author=Gina De Angelis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=daHmkclqERYC&q=Lumi%C3%A8re+Besan%C3%A7on+Lyon&pg=PA34 |title=Motion Pictures |publisher=The Oliver Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-1-881508-78-6}}</ref>

The Lumière brothers' primary business interests were in selling cameras and film equipment to exhibitors, not the actual production of films. Despite this, filmmakers across the world were inspired by the potential of film as exhibitors brought their shows to new countries. 

In the process of filming actualities, especially those of real events, filmmakers discovered and experimented with multiple camera techniques to accommodate for their unpredictable nature.<ref>{{Cite book |editor=Tom Elsaesser |url=http://archive.org/details/earlycinemaspace0000unse |title=Early cinema: space, frame, narrative |date=1990 |publisher=London : BFI Pub. |isbn=978-0-85170-244-5}}</ref>

[[File:La Fée aux Choux.webm|thumb|A 1900 restaging of the 1897 film ''[[La Fée aux Choux]]'', directed by [[Alice Guy]]]]
Experiments in film editing, special effects, narrative construction, and camera movement during this period by filmmakers in France, England, and the United States became influential in establishing an identity for film going forward. At both the Edison and Lumière studios, loose narratives such as the 1895 Edison film, ''Washday Troubles,'' established short relationship dynamics and simple storylines.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bohn |first=Thomas W. |url=http://archive.org/details/lightshadowshist0000bohn_a8u0 |title=Light and shadows: a history of motion pictures |date=1987 |publisher=Palo Alto, Calif. : Mayfield Pub.
